common_errors.hip_dropping: Allowing the hips to sag toward the floor on the way out — the equivalent of sagging in a plank and for the same reason. The abdominals must isometrically brace against gravity to keep the spine neutral; hip drop means they have disengaged and the lumbar extensors are now passively carrying the load.
common_errors.overreaching_too_soon: Rolling out further than the current core strength level allows, which forces the lumbar spine into hyperextension to compensate. The rollout distance should be limited to what the athlete can control with a neutral spine; premature overreach is the primary injury mechanism for ab wheel-related low back strains.
common_errors.elbow_bending: Bending the elbows rather than keeping them relatively straight throughout the roll-out. This converts an anti-extension core drill into a partial pull exercise that unloads the abs and shifts the challenge to the triceps and lats without providing the intended stimulus.
common_errors.insufficient_return: Using momentum or a partial pullback rather than truly returning to the starting position under muscular control. The concentric phase should be as deliberate as the eccentric; failure to fully return prevents full engagement of the abdominals at the shortened end of the range.
common_errors.neck_strain: Craning the neck to look forward during the rollout rather than maintaining neutral cervical alignment. This adds unnecessary cervical compressive loading and is usually a symptom of overall core fatigue — a cue to terminate the set rather than compensate.

common_errors.rotating_before_pressing: Performing the wrist rotation as a distinct preparatory move before initiating the press disconnects the movement and eliminates its continuous-tension advantage. The rotation and the press should occur simultaneously in one smooth arc — this is the technical signature of the Arnold and what makes it more effective than a standard press.
common_errors.elbows_dropping_too_low: Allowing the elbows to drop to the abdomen at the bottom (as if completing a full bicep curl) takes tension off the deltoids and shifts it onto the biceps as a loaded stretch. The elbows should hang in front of the chest at the bottom, not pointing toward the floor, so the delts remain under tension throughout.
common_errors.excessive_load: Because the Arnold press demands control through multiple planes simultaneously, loading it as heavily as a strict dumbbell press inevitably compromises the rotation, causes lateral body lean, and may impinge the shoulder. EMG research shows superior deltoid activation at moderate loads — this is a hypertrophy exercise, not a max-strength movement.
common_errors.torso_lean_or_lumbar_hyperextension: Arching the lower back and using spinal extension to assist the press under fatigue is common as weight increases or sets get long. This shifts load to the lower back and reduces deltoid stimulus. A braced core and upright torso are required; a reduction in load is always preferable to compensation.
common_errors.asymmetrical_rotation: One hand rotating faster than the other, or one shoulder lacking the mobility to complete the supination-to-pronation arc, creates uneven loading and can stress the rotator cuff on the less mobile side. This is often a symptom of internal rotation stiffness and should be addressed with mobility work before loading the movement.

common_errors.incorrect_seat_height: Seat set too low forces the knee into excessive flexion at the bottom of the pedal stroke, placing the hip flexors and quads at a mechanical disadvantage and dramatically reducing power output per stroke. At the correct height, the knee should have a slight bend — approximately 5–10 degrees — when the pedal is at its lowest point, allowing for near-full leg extension and maximal force application.
common_errors.passive_arm_engagement: Holding the handles loosely and allowing the arms to move passively rather than actively pushing and pulling through the full range of motion eliminates the upper body training stimulus and cuts total power output by 20–30% compared to full engagement. The athlete should drive the handles forward with the chest and triceps during the push phase and pull aggressively with the lats, rhomboids, and biceps during the pull phase — the arms should be working as hard as the legs.
common_errors.knee_valgus_under_fatigue: The knees collapsing inward toward each other as the athlete fatigues reduces the mechanical efficiency of each pedal stroke and places abnormal stress on the medial knee structures. Coaches should cue athletes to keep the knees tracking directly in line with the toes throughout the entire set, and should reduce load or interval duration if form breaks down.
common_errors.going_out_too_fast_in_interval_work: Sprinting at absolute maximum effort on the first interval of a protocol such as 10 rounds of 30-seconds-on/30-seconds-off inevitably leads to a steep decline in output across subsequent rounds — the tenth interval may produce only 40–50% of the first. The goal for interval work is consistent repeatable power, not a single peak, so athletes should start at 85–90% of maximum sustainable effort and hold that number across all rounds.
common_errors.forward_head_and_rounded_shoulders: Allowing the head to jut forward and the upper back to round under heavy effort is common but reduces breathing efficiency, increases neck and upper trap fatigue, and limits power transfer from the torso into the handles. The athlete should maintain a neutral spine, keep the chest up, and think about driving the crown of the head toward the ceiling throughout the effort.

common_errors.hands_directly_under_stone: Gripping with hands directly under the stone's equator rather than slightly forward at the 10 and 2 o'clock positions forces the biceps to bear the majority of the load rather than using the chest, lat, and forearm friction. This is both mechanically weaker and the primary mechanism of bicipital tendon injuries, which are the most commonly reported atlas stone injury site in strongman research.
common_errors.lapping_too_low: Getting the stone only to knee height before attempting to sit and lap rather than deadlifting it as high as possible first — a higher initial pull before lapping gives the athlete a larger margin to roll the stone up the thighs and reduces the second pull distance required to load or clear a bar.
common_errors.hips_before_hip_drive: Attempting to stand up before hip extension sequence is complete: the first pull phase must load the hip extensors before the back extensors fire, as per McGill's EMG analysis of the event. Athletes who extend the back first under load place the lumbar spine in maximum flexion at peak moment, creating the conditions for disc injury.
common_errors.stance_too_narrow_or_too_wide: Feet set too close together eliminate the ability to lap the stone effectively because knees block forearm travel; feet too wide reduce the hip drive velocity needed for the second pull. The ideal stance allows the athlete to see both feet on either side of the stone, per coaching consensus from multiple WSM competitors.
common_errors.hugging_at_center_for_high_platforms: When loading stones to tall platforms, re-gripping at the stone's horizontal equator limits the range of upward extension available. Hands must be positioned above the stone's center for tall loads so the final hip-extend-and-roll maneuver can clear the platform height — athletes who fail to adjust grip for platform height consistently stall at the lip.

common_errors.hyperextending_at_top: Extending past neutral spine at the top of the movement — the goal is to reach a straight line from head to heel, not to arch the back further. Hyperextension compresses posterior spinal structures and shifts load from the posterior chain to the lumbar facet joints.
common_errors.momentum_and_bouncing: Using a rapid, jerky movement rather than controlled concentric and eccentric phases — ballistic back extensions place extreme shear forces on the intervertebral discs and ligaments. Each rep should be deliberate with at least a 2-second lowering phase.
common_errors.glute_exclusion: Focusing exclusively on spinal extension while neglecting hip extension — athletes who cue only 'back muscles' generate most of the movement through lumbar flexion-extension rather than hip hinge mechanics. Cueing 'squeeze glutes at the top' significantly shifts activation toward the posterior chain.
common_errors.rounding_on_descent: Losing neutral spine during the lowering phase, flexing the lumbar region excessively — the disc is most vulnerable under combined flexion and load. The descent should maintain a neutral or slightly extended spine throughout.
common_errors.cervical_hyperextension: Looking upward and hyperextending the neck rather than maintaining a neutral cervical spine aligned with the thoracic spine. This is especially common in athletes trying to use their head position to generate momentum.

common_errors.hip_flexion: Bending at the hips as the body lowers rather than keeping them fully extended, which reduces hamstring activation and converts the movement into a hip hinge instead of a knee-flexion eccentric. Hips must remain locked in extension throughout the descent so all eccentric work is borne by the hamstrings across the knee joint.
common_errors.gripping_band_too_high_eliminating_chall: Holding the band very high or with excess tension so it assists most of the descent, making the exercise so easy that the hamstrings receive insufficient training stimulus. The band should reduce the load just enough for the athlete to control the eccentric to a point below where they'd fail unassisted — the bottom third should still be genuinely challenging.
common_errors.collapsing_too_fast_in_lower_range: Dropping quickly through the hardest portion of the movement (lower half), despite having band assistance, and losing eccentric hamstring tension. Athletes need to be cued to actively resist the descent throughout, not just until fatigue causes collapse, and then utilize the band to help return.
common_errors.using_arms_to_push_back_up: Relying on a push-up motion from the floor on the concentric phase rather than using hamstring concentric strength to return to the start position, even with the band helping. Pushing aggressively off the floor should be treated as a reset rather than an active concentric repetition, and the band provides the appropriate assistance so excessive arm push-off is unnecessary.
common_errors.unsecured_ankles: Insufficient ankle fixation allowing the anchor to shift during the rep, which lets the body shift forward and unloads the hamstrings mid-set. Regardless of the setup — Nordic bench, barbell, partner, or lat pulldown pad — the feet must be firmly and consistently anchored to maintain the closed-chain nature of the exercise.

common_errors.upper_trap_shrugging: Letting the shoulders elevate toward the ears during the pull, which shifts load from the target muscles — middle and lower trapezius, rear delts — onto the upper trapezius and neck. The coaching cue is retract AND depress the scapulae simultaneously, not just squeeze them together.
common_errors.band_too_heavy: Using a band with too much resistance forces the arms to bend at the elbows and involves the triceps, turning a scapular exercise into a pressing movement. The band should be light enough to maintain nearly straight elbows and feel the retraction, not the elbow extension.
common_errors.excessive_speed: Rushing through repetitions eliminates the time under tension that makes this exercise effective for neuromuscular re-education and postural endurance. A controlled 2-second pull and 4-second return tempo dramatically increases stimulus quality.
common_errors.no_end_range_pause: Failing to pause when the band reaches the chest eliminates peak contraction of the middle trapezius and rhomboids. A 1–2 second hold at end range dramatically increases the training stimulus for scapular retractors.
common_errors.internal_rotation_default: Performing all repetitions palm-down (pronated) trains the movement exclusively in internal rotation, missing the infraspinatus and lower trapezius activation that palm-up (supinated) position provides. In populations with anterior shoulder dominance this perpetuates the imbalance the exercise is prescribed to correct.

common_errors.weak_brace: Failing to create adequate intra-abdominal pressure before descent — this destabilizes the entire spine and trunk, making the lift mechanically inefficient and dramatically increasing injury risk to the lower back. Cue: take a big breath, brace your core as if about to take a punch, then descend.
common_errors.excessive_forward_lean: Torso collapsing forward during descent, resembling a good morning — occurs when the athlete lacks anterior core strength or uses too much weight, shifting the load entirely onto the lower back instead of distributing it through the legs and hips.
common_errors.knee_valgus: Knees caving toward the midline during the descent or ascent — indicates weak hip abductors (gluteus medius) and significantly increases ACL injury risk while reducing force production from the glutes. Cue: 'push knees out over little toes.'
common_errors.hips_rising_first: Hips shoot up before the bar moves off the bottom position, commonly called the 'stripper squat' — caused by weak quadriceps or poor setup, effectively turning the squat into a stiff-leg deadlift and overloading the lumbar spine.
common_errors.insufficient_depth: Not reaching parallel (hip crease failing to drop below the top of the knee) — reduces gluteus maximus activation and eliminates the full range-of-motion benefits, often caused by ankle or hip mobility limitations or habitually training with too much weight.

common_errors.elbow_flare: Allowing the elbows to flare out perpendicular to the torso instead of maintaining roughly a 45–75° tuck angle — excessive flare dramatically increases anterior shoulder stress and impingement risk by placing the humerus in a mechanically disadvantaged abducted position, particularly dangerous under heavy loads.
common_errors.bouncing_bar_off_chest: Letting the bar free-fall and using elastic rebound off the sternum rather than a controlled touch-and-go or pause — this removes muscular control during the most loaded portion of the lift, shifts stress to the sternocostal cartilage and ribs, and teaches poor eccentric mechanics that limit strength development.
common_errors.loss_of_upper_back_tightness: Failing to retract and depress the scapulae and maintain a stable upper-back platform throughout the set — a flat or shifting upper back eliminates the stable pressing surface, reduces force transfer, and shifts stress directly onto the anterior shoulder capsule and pec tendons.
common_errors.bar_path_error: Pressing straight up toward the ceiling rather than in a slight arc back toward the rack — the optimal bar path closes the horizontal distance between the bar and shoulder joint early in the ascent, reducing the moment arm and making the lockout mechanically easier; a purely vertical path is inefficient and common in untrained lifters.
common_errors.butt_lift: Raising the glutes off the bench to reduce the bar's travel distance — this creates uncontrolled hyperextension of the lumbar spine under load and eliminates the stable base needed for leg drive, shifting stress to the lower back and providing a false sense of load capacity.
common_errors.wrist_extension: Allowing the wrists to hyperextend backward so the bar sits in the fingers rather than in the heel of the hand over the forearm — this dissipates force transfer into the bar, creates significant wrist joint pain under load, and can cause chronic wrist pathology over time.

common_errors.elbow_drift_forward: The elbows creep forward at the top of the movement instead of staying pinned to the sides — this transfers load to the anterior deltoid and reduces peak biceps contraction. Keeping elbows stationary at the sides ensures the biceps complete the full range of contraction.
common_errors.excessive_body_swing: Using lumbar hyperextension and hip thrust to generate momentum is the most common compensation when the load is too heavy. This unloads the biceps at the most critical portion of the rep and shifts force demands to the lower back, increasing injury risk.
common_errors.short_range_of_motion: Failing to fully extend the elbows at the bottom or fully flex at the top eliminates the loaded stretch and peak contraction — both of which are key drivers of hypertrophy. A full ROM from full elbow extension to forearm contact with the biceps is the clinical standard.
common_errors.uncontrolled_eccentric: Dropping the bar rapidly on the descent abandons the eccentric phase, which EMG and hypertrophy research consistently identifies as the higher-damage and higher-growth portion of the rep. A 2–3 second controlled descent significantly increases training stimulus.
common_errors.wrist_extension: Allowing the wrists to hyperextend (break backward) under load transfers stress to the wrist flexors and reduces the mechanical efficiency of the curl. A neutral wrist held in line with the forearm keeps the load on the elbow flexors where it belongs.

common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: Arching the lower back excessively at the top of the movement — the athlete substitutes lumbar extension for true hip extension because the glutes aren't firing adequately. This risks lower back injury and means the glutes are not receiving the intended stimulus. Cue: 'ribs down, posteriorly tilt the pelvis at the top.'
common_errors.incomplete_lockout: Failing to achieve full hip extension at the top of the movement — reduces gluteus maximus activation at the shortened position and defeats the primary purpose of the exercise. The hips should form a straight line with the knees and shoulders at lockout.
common_errors.neck_hyperextension: Cranking the head back to look at the ceiling during the thrust — creates unnecessary cervical spine stress throughout the set. The neck should remain neutral, aligned with the torso.
common_errors.bench_height_error: Bench positioned too low or too high, altering the mechanics of the movement — optimal height places the mid-scapula on the bench edge when the hips are extended. Too low reduces range of motion; too high shifts load to the lower back.
common_errors.bar_rolling: Failing to secure the barbell properly with a pad and grip, allowing it to roll during the set — breaks the movement pattern, creates distraction, and can cause bruising or injury to the anterior hip. Always use a hip thrust pad and maintain a firm grip on the bar.

common_errors.lumbar_flexion_under_load: Allowing the lower back to round during the pull — this shifts compressive and shear force onto the intervertebral discs and posterior ligaments rather than distributing it through the musculature, creating significant injury risk. A neutral lumbar spine must be braced and maintained before the bar leaves the floor.
common_errors.excessive_torso_oscillation: Using a hip drive or torso bounce to generate momentum rather than initiating purely from the upper back musculature — this is most common when the load exceeds the athlete's back strength, turning a horizontal row into a partial Romanian deadlift and dramatically reducing rhomboid, trap, and lat stimulus.
common_errors.insufficient_scapular_retraction_at_top: Pulling the bar to the torso but failing to fully retract and depress the scapulae at peak contraction — the bar reaching the body does not guarantee the target muscles have fully shortened. Cue athletes to squeeze the shoulder blades toward the spine at the top of every rep.
common_errors.elbows_flaring_excessively: Allowing the elbows to travel 90° out from the torso rather than tracking at approximately 45–60° — extreme elbow flare shifts load from the lats and mid-traps toward the posterior deltoids and can compress the shoulder impingement zone under load.
common_errors.bar_drifting_forward: The bar pulling away from the body throughout the range of motion rather than traveling vertically — this lengthens the moment arm continuously and exponentially increases lower back stress, particularly at the point of maximal spinal load.

common_errors.standing_too_close_to_anchor: Standing so close that the rope is taut from the start — this creates excessive tension that forces a hunched, bent-over posture to counterbalance and significantly degrades wave quality. The athlete should step 1–3 paces forward to create enough slack so waves travel cleanly down the full length of the rope to the anchor.
common_errors.arms_only_movement: Generating waves exclusively from the arms and shoulders without involving the legs and hips — this severely limits power output, creates rapid local muscular fatigue before any meaningful cardiovascular training stimulus is achieved, and produces short choppy waves that lose energy before reaching the anchor. The movement should originate from a partial squat with the feet, legs, and hips driving power upward through the torso and into the rope.
common_errors.overgripping_handles: Squeezing the handles with maximum grip force throughout the set prematurely exhausts the forearms and limits the duration and quality of effective training. The grip should be firm enough to control the rope but no tighter — coaches often cue athletes to hold the handle the way they would hold a small animal: secure but not crushing.
common_errors.poor_postural_position: Allowing the shoulders to round forward, the chest to collapse inward, and the spine to flex under fatigue — this increases the risk of shoulder impingement and lower back strain while also reducing core engagement and limiting the power that can transfer from the lower body into the ropes. The cue is tall spine, proud chest, shoulders wide and back, weight sitting into an athletic quarter-squat.
common_errors.short_choppy_waves: Producing small rapid movements that never travel the full length of the rope indicates the athlete is not generating sufficient power from the legs and hips and is relying entirely on wrist and forearm action. Effective waves should be large, fluid, and reach the anchor point on every repetition — if they die out halfway, the athlete should slow down, reset their stance, and focus on driving from the hips.

aliases: quadruped opposite arm and leg raise

common_errors.lumbar_extension_substitution: Achieving the appearance of leg elevation by hyperextending the lumbar spine rather than through genuine hip extension. This is the most clinically significant error because it loads the lumbar facets and posterior disc, the exact structures the bird dog is typically prescribed to protect. The leg should be in line with the torso, not raised above it.
common_errors.hip_rotation: Rotating the pelvis toward the ceiling as the leg lifts — a common compensation driven by hip flexor tightness or insufficient hip extension range. The hips must remain square and level throughout; coaches cue athletes to imagine a cup of water balanced on the lower back that cannot be spilled.
common_errors.rushing_through_holds: Moving in and out of the extended position rapidly rather than developing a stable hold before each rep. The neuromuscular stabilization benefit requires the athlete to find and maintain the locked position; speed through the movement bypasses this entirely and trains little beyond coordination.
common_errors.elevated_limb_position: Raising the arm above ear height or the leg significantly above hip height in an attempt to increase apparent range of motion. Higher is not better here — the exercise becomes compromised at any height that creates spinal deviation, and most athletes cannot maintain neutral alignment with limbs raised more than parallel to the floor.
common_errors.weight_shifting: Rocking side-to-side onto the loaded arm or leg rather than distributing weight evenly through all four points during the preparatory phase. This is a compensation for limited single-leg/arm balance ability and reduces the core stabilization demand to near zero before the extension phase even begins.

common_errors.torso_elevation: Allowing the torso to tilt upward into lumbar extension rather than remaining parallel to the floor — identified by Seedman (Advanced Human Performance) as the single most prevalent error. When the torso rises and the extended leg drops, anterior core and multifidus demand collapses and load shifts to passive lumbar structures, creating the very spinal compression the exercise is designed to prevent.
common_errors.hip_rotation: Rotating or opening the hips toward the ceiling as the leg extends or as the weight is rowed — the pelvis twists toward the rowing-arm side. This compensatory pattern offloads hip external rotator demand, eliminates anti-rotation core engagement, and converts the movement into a simple single-arm row. Correction: the hip of the extended leg must remain internally rotated with the knee pointing straight down throughout.
common_errors.excessive_momentum_top_rock: Using lateral sway or a body-English heave to swing the weight up at the top of the row rather than pulling with lat, rhomboid, and rear delt. In the quadruped position momentum is theoretically self-limiting, but lifters compensate by collapsing the support-arm elbow or swaying the torso sideways. The coaching cue is to pause with the dumbbell off the floor, establish core set position, and initiate a strict pull with scapular retraction before the row begins.
common_errors.weight_too_heavy: Selecting a load the lifter cannot control at the tempo required for spinal stability. Unlike bilateral rows where momentum and hip drive absorb excess load, the bird dog row has no such escape valve — excessive weight immediately manifests as hip rotation, torso elevation, or lateral spinal bend. Cressey Sports Performance programs this exercise at 6–10 controlled reps per side; form degradation before set completion is the primary indicator that load exceeds capacity.
common_errors.support_arm_collapse: Allowing the support-arm shoulder to passively sink toward the bench rather than actively pressing away from it. This deactivates the serratus anterior and eliminates the concurrent activation potentiation (CAP/irradiation) effect: intense grip and shoulder activation in the support limb drives neural output to the core musculature throughout the kinetic chain. The support hand must grip the bench firmly and push away from it, keeping the scapula packed down on the ribcage.
common_errors.leg_drop_during_row: Allowing the extended leg to sag below hip height as cognitive attention shifts to the rowing motion. Because the gluteus maximus must maintain isometric hip extension for the full set, fatigue or inattention causes the leg to drop — which reduces posterior oblique sling tension (the contralateral lat-to-glute connection through the thoracolumbar fascia) and degrades the exercise from a full-body integration drill into an isolated row. The extended leg and the rowing arm must reach their peak position simultaneously and hold there.

common_errors.box_too_high: Using a box height that forces a deep landing squat — this demonstrates hip mobility, not jump height, and dramatically increases joint stress on landing. The box should be set to a height the athlete can land in an athletic quarter-squat position, not a full squat.
common_errors.knee_valgus_on_landing: Knees caving inward at takeoff or landing, which dramatically increases ACL stress and is especially prevalent in female athletes. Both the push-off and landing positions should have knees tracking over the second and third toes.
common_errors.not_achieving_full_extension: Failing to fully extend hips and knees at the top of the box — the movement is not complete until the athlete is fully upright. In CrossFit contexts this is an explicit no-rep standard, and in power training it eliminates the full triple-extension stimulus.
common_errors.loud_stomping_landing: Absorbing ground contact noisily, indicating the athlete is not loading the muscles eccentrically and is instead dumping force into the joints. Athletes should land soft and controlled, with the glutes and quads absorbing the impact over multiple joints.
common_errors.rebounding_immediately: Jumping back down and immediately rebounding to the next rep — this places extreme stress on the Achilles tendon and has caused documented ruptures, and shifts the exercise from power development to a conditioning drill that accumulates fatigue and degrades jump mechanics.

common_errors.excessive_forward_lean: Torso collapsing forward over the front knee — typically indicates too much weight or insufficient hip flexor flexibility in the rear leg, and shifts emphasis away from the quadriceps onto the lower back. Cue: 'chest tall, descend straight down.'
common_errors.rear_leg_pushing: Using the rear foot to push off the bench and assist the lift — defeats the unilateral purpose of the exercise by offloading the working leg. The rear foot should rest lightly on the bench for balance only.
common_errors.knee_valgus: Front knee caving inward during the descent — indicates weak gluteus medius and increases patellofemoral and ACL stress. Cue: 'screw your front foot into the floor' to engage external hip rotation and push the knee out.
common_errors.stance_length_error: Front foot positioned too close to or too far from the bench — too close limits depth and overloads the knee past the toes; too far reduces quad engagement and puts excessive strain on the hip flexors of the rear leg.
common_errors.losing_balance: Swaying laterally or the rear foot slipping mid-rep — indicates the movement pattern is not yet grooved or the load is too heavy for current stability. Athletes should master bodyweight before adding external load.

common_errors.wrong_pulley_height_for_goal: Most lifters default to mid-chest height regardless of intent. High-pulley cables (hands pulling low-to-high) preferentially load the clavicular head; low-pulley cables (high-to-low path) load the sternal and costal fibers. Using one height exclusively guarantees partial pec development.
common_errors.elbow_bending_to_move_more_weight: Bending the elbows to a significant angle converts the fly into a partial cable press, reducing the moment arm and taking load off the pectorals entirely. Elbows should maintain a consistent soft bend (10–20 degrees) throughout the movement and that angle should never change.
common_errors.leaning_so_far_forward_that_posterior_ch: Excessive forward lean to increase range of motion destabilizes the pelvis and lower back, creating a movement that resembles a standing good morning. The torso lean should be minimal and consistent—the chest should naturally feel the stretch, not the hamstrings.
common_errors.cable_handles_touching_and_releasing_ten: Touching the handles together or allowing them to swing through, as with a rapid crossover motion, eliminates peak contraction tension. Stopping just before contact and holding the isometric peak for a beat provides superior pectoral stimulation.
common_errors.shoulder_protraction_at_lockout: Rounding the shoulders forward at the end range to extend the range of motion places the glenohumeral joint in a vulnerable anterior-loaded position. Scapular retraction should be maintained throughout; reach for chest squeeze by squeezing the pecs, not by protruding the shoulders.

common_errors.hip_flexion_dominance: Hinging forward from the hips rather than curling the spine — the most pervasive cable crunch error. When the hips move, the hip flexors perform the work and the rectus abdominis is largely bypassed. The cue is to keep the thighs absolutely perpendicular to the floor while the ribcage curls toward the pelvis through spinal flexion only.
common_errors.arms_pulling_the_load: Using the arms to yank the rope downward rather than keeping them fixed so that the abdominals are the sole movers. The hands should hold the rope at a fixed position beside the head throughout; any movement in the elbows indicates the arms are driving the rep.
common_errors.insufficient_range: Crunching only partway down and missing the full spinal flexion that maximizes rectus abdominis contraction. The target is to bring the elbows toward the knees and feel a peak contraction in the lower abdominals at the bottom of the movement.
common_errors.standing_too_close: Positioning the body too near the cable stack, which reduces the counterbalancing tension needed to keep the hips stationary. Stepping 2-3 feet back from the machine creates the correct line of pull and allows the abdominals to resist the cable rather than the hip flexors managing the balance task.
common_errors.too_heavy_too_soon: Loading more weight than the rectus abdominis can control, which predictably results in hip flexion compensation and arm pulling. Cable crunches are most effective with moderate weight at high control; ego loading defeats every technical requirement simultaneously.

cable external rotation at 90 degrees abduction

common_errors.elbow_drift: Allowing the elbow to move away from the torso during the rotation shifts the movement from a pure external rotation exercise into a combination of abduction and rotation, reducing infraspinatus isolation and increasing deltoid contribution. The elbow must remain pinned to the side throughout the entire movement.
common_errors.wrist_drop: Letting the wrist drop below the elbow plane as the hand moves away collapses the neutral forearm position and reduces the torque angle on the external rotators — the hand must stay level with or above the elbow throughout the arc.
common_errors.excessive_load: Loading too heavy forces the upper trapezius and posterior deltoid to dominate, often accompanied by scapular elevation and trunk rotation, bypassing the small rotator cuff muscles entirely. This exercise should feel like a controlled, isolated burn with light weight, not a strength grind.
common_errors.scapular_movement: Allowing the scapula to retract excessively as the arm externally rotates recruits the middle trapezius and rhomboids as prime movers and reduces the glenohumeral isolation. Cue the athlete to hold the shoulder blade still — the movement comes from the shoulder joint only.
common_errors.trunk_rotation_compensation: Rotating the torso away from the cable to increase apparent range of motion substitutes for true glenohumeral external rotation — the torso must remain square throughout, and range should be limited to whatever the shoulder joint can produce independently.

common_errors.lateral_trunk_lean: Bending the torso toward or away from the cable stack to assist the lift — this offloads the abductors by substituting trunk side-flexion for hip abduction, defeating the purpose of isolating the gluteus medius. The torso should remain upright and still throughout the entire rep.
common_errors.momentum_and_swinging: Using a kicking or ballistic motion to swing the leg rather than moving it with slow, controlled muscular force — swinging recruits the hip flexors and reduces time under tension for the gluteus medius, which is the intended primary mover.
common_errors.excessive_range_of_motion: Lifting the leg too high (typically beyond 45–60 degrees), which causes the pelvis to hike and recruits the quadratus lumborum and trunk lateral flexors instead of keeping the work in the abductor — peak gluteus medius tension occurs well before end-range.
common_errors.knee_and_foot_rotation: Allowing the working leg to externally or internally rotate during the movement changes the muscular demand; EMG research shows that slight internal rotation of the hip preferentially increases gluteus medius activation relative to TFL, so thoughtless foot positioning compromises targeting.
common_errors.too_much_weight: Loading the cable beyond what allows proper form causes compensatory trunk lean and momentum to dominate the movement, shifting stress away from the lateral hip to the lower back and reducing gluteal stimulus.

common_errors.trunk_rotation_and_lean: Rotating the torso or bending away from the direction of pull to help swing the leg across the body — this substitutes trunk movement for adductor contraction and places unnecessary rotational stress on the lumbar spine.
common_errors.excessive_crossover_range: Pulling the leg excessively far across the midline beyond a natural adduction endpoint puts the medial knee and hip in a compromised position and takes tension off the adductors at the shortened end of the range.
common_errors.momentum_over_muscle: Using a ballistic swinging motion rather than slow controlled adduction reduces adductor time under tension significantly and often recruits hip flexors to assist, which is especially problematic for groin strain rehabilitation contexts.
common_errors.unstable_stance_leg: Failing to maintain a slightly bent, braced stance leg allows the pelvis to tilt and the body to wobble, which both reduces adductor isolation and increases fall risk especially at higher loads.
common_errors.too_much_load: Overloading the cable forces compensatory momentum and trunk lean rather than controlled adductor contraction — adductors are strong but this is a single-joint isolation movement that rewards controlled tempo over maximal load.

aliases: cable internal rotation at 90 degrees abduction

common_errors.elbow_drift: Allowing the elbow to move forward and away from the torso as the hand moves across the body transforms the exercise from an isolated subscapularis drill into a horizontal adduction movement dominated by the pectoralis major. The elbow must remain pressed against the side throughout.
common_errors.excessive_range_of_motion: Pulling the hand past the midline of the body and into end-range internal rotation creates impingement risk at the anterior shoulder and loads the anterior capsule beyond safe limits. The movement should stop when the forearm is perpendicular to the torso.
common_errors.trunk_rotation_compensation: Rotating the torso inward to add apparent range of motion is one of the most common errors, especially as weight increases — it substitutes large trunk muscle contribution for the intended subscapularis isolation. The torso must stay square and still.
common_errors.load_too_heavy: The subscapularis is significantly stronger than the external rotators, making it tempting to load heavily, but excessive weight shifts control to the larger global movers (pec, anterior deltoid, lat) and defeats the purpose of the isolated rehab exercise.
common_errors.asymmetric_programming: Prescribing internal rotation without a matching external rotation volume — or vice versa — is a common clinical error that perpetuates the rotational strength imbalances it is meant to correct. The external-to-internal rotation strength ratio (typically 2:3) must guide loading decisions.

common_errors.arm_pulling: Using the arms to pull the rope forward rather than driving with the hips — the arms and rope should be passive conduits of force generated by hip extension. When the arms pull, the lats and biceps take over and the posterior chain disengages.
common_errors.squat_pattern_substitution: Bending the knees excessively and using a squat pattern instead of a hip hinge — this converts a posterior chain exercise into a quad-dominant movement. The hinge requires the hips to push back while the knees remain relatively extended.
common_errors.standing_too_close: Setting up too close to the cable stack limits the backward hip travel needed to create a loaded hinge position, compressing the range of motion and reducing the stretch on the hamstrings and glutes.
common_errors.standing_too_far: Standing so far that the cable tension is too high at the start position — the athlete can't initiate from a proper hinge, and the loading becomes awkward. Optimal distance creates meaningful tension through the full ROM.
common_errors.lower_back_rounding: Losing lumbar neutral during the hinge, particularly as fatigue accumulates or weight increases. The lower back should remain in a braced, neutral arch throughout — rounding shifts load from the glutes and hamstrings to the spinal erectors and discs.
common_errors.not_hinging_deep_enough: A shallow hip hinge that never fully loads the posterior chain — the athlete must push the hips back far enough to feel a hamstring stretch before driving forward. Insufficient depth defeats the purpose of the movement.

common_errors.treating_it_as_a_biceps_curl: Initiating and dominating the movement with elbow flexion rather than lat-driven shoulder extension and adduction — the biceps are a powerful synergist here but should not be the primary mover. Cue: think about pulling your elbows down to your back pockets, not curling your hands to your shoulders.
common_errors.scapular_elevation_at_initiation: Starting each rep without first setting the scapulae in a depressed and slightly retracted position — identical to pull-up error mechanics, this bypasses lat engagement and increases upper trap and neck loading from the very first inch of the pull.
common_errors.incomplete_range_of_motion: Not fully extending the elbows at the bottom of each rep — common because the supinated grip makes the stretched position feel more vulnerable, but full elbow extension is required to train the lat and biceps through their full functional range.
common_errors.forward_head_compensation: Jutting the chin forward rather than keeping the neck neutral to reach the top position — indicates the athlete is very close to their load ceiling and should consider adding assisted reps or reducing load rather than compromising cervical alignment.
common_errors.grip_width_too_wide: Positioning hands wider than shoulder width in a supinated grip — this externally rotates the forearm into a biomechanically weak and potentially injurious position at the wrist and elbow. Chin-up grip should be at or narrower than shoulder width.

common_errors.pelvic_rotation: Allowing the top hip to roll backward as the knee rises — this is the single most common fault and is often invisible to the lifter without tactile feedback; placing a hand on the iliac crest to monitor pelvic position is a key clinical cue, as any rolling immediately shifts work from the glutes to the lumbar rotators.
common_errors.knee_not_reaching_sufficient_height: Only lifting the knee a few inches rather than rotating through the full available external rotation range reduces the gluteal stimulus significantly — the goal is maximum hip ER within the neutral pelvic constraint, not just any upward movement.
common_errors.hip_angle_too_flat: Performing the exercise with less than 45–60 degrees of hip flexion reduces posterior gluteus medius activation; EMG literature confirms that moderate hip flexion (30–60 degrees) produces higher GMed activity in the posterior segment than a neutral or extended hip position.
common_errors.muscle_not_activated_at_all: Many lifters perform high-rep clamshells without generating meaningful fatigue because the glutes are not truly activated — if the exercise feels easy before 20 reps, the band resistance is too low, the range is restricted, or compensation is occurring. True clamshells with proper technique should produce a burning sensation in the posterior gluteus medius within 10–15 reps.
common_errors.asymmetry_unaddressed: Not checking for and correcting side-to-side differences in external rotation range or activation strength — the clamshell is particularly useful for identifying unilateral weakness, so comparing both sides each session is essential for its rehabilitative purpose.

common_errors.bar_path_not_s_curve: Pulling the bar in a straight vertical line rather than the clean's characteristic S-curve (toward the body past the knees, slightly forward at the hip brush, then vertical at extension) breaks bar-body contact and reduces force transfer to the bar.
common_errors.hips_rising_faster_than_shoulders: When hips lead the shoulders up from the floor, the lifter ends up in a mechanically poor Romanian deadlift posture before the second pull rather than an upright position ready for hip explosion; shoulders and hips must maintain their relative angle through the first pull.
common_errors.early_shoulder_elevation: Beginning the trapezius shrug before full triple extension is reached reduces the time available for the legs and hips to accelerate the bar; the shrug is the final exclamation point of full extension, not a substitute for it.
common_errors.loading_through_the_toes: Shifting weight forward onto the toes during the second pull causes the lifter to jump forward, wastes force horizontally, and trains a movement pattern that will consistently place the catch in front of the body rather than under it.
common_errors.treating_it_like_a_deadlift: Performing the clean pull slowly under control from floor to hip rather than using distinct tempo changes (deliberate first pull, explosive second pull) removes the neuromuscular adaptation benefit and defeats the purpose of the exercise as a strength-speed drill.

common_errors.grip_too_narrow: Placing the hands inside shoulder width (thumbs touching or index fingers touching) increases wrist ulnar deviation and elbow torque dramatically. Research supports a grip width of approximately 95–100% of biacromial distance as optimal; anything narrower compromises joint health without adding meaningful tricep emphasis.
common_errors.elbow_flare: Allowing the elbows to travel out to the sides negates the close grip's tricep emphasis and shifts load back to the chest, effectively turning it into a conventional bench press. Elbows should stay tucked close to the torso throughout the movement.
common_errors.bar_path_to_high_on_chest: Lowering the bar to the clavicles or upper chest shortens the effective range of elbow extension and places unnecessary stress on the AC joint. The bar should descend to the lower sternum, mirroring where the elbows are most mechanically efficient.
common_errors.wrist_breakdown: Wrists frequently collapse backward under load because the neutral hand position of the close grip is less stable. The wrist must stay stacked directly over the elbow throughout; wrist wraps can help beginners learn the position before it becomes habitual.
common_errors.insufficient_lockout: Stopping short of full elbow extension eliminates peak contraction of the triceps brachii, which is precisely what this lift is programmed to build. Unless performing deliberate partial-range work, the rep should finish at complete lockout.

common_errors.rounded_lower_back: Lumbar flexion under load — increases the distance the bar must travel and places enormous shearing force on the spinal discs. This is the primary mechanism of deadlift-related injury and must be corrected before adding any load. Cue: 'proud chest, push the floor away.'
common_errors.hips_too_low: Setting up with hips well below the optimal position, essentially squatting the deadlift — pushes the bar forward of the midfoot, creates an inefficient lever arm, and reduces posterior chain engagement. The hip angle should allow a straight bar path over the midfoot.
common_errors.hips_rising_early: Hips shoot up before the bar breaks the floor — indicates weak quadriceps or improper starting position, immediately converting the pull to a stiff-leg deadlift and overloading the lower back through the most vulnerable portion of the lift.
common_errors.bar_drifting_forward: Bar path moves away from the shins and body during the pull — occurs when the lats aren't engaged to 'protect the armpits,' creating a massive moment arm and dramatically increasing lower back stress. Cue: 'drag the bar up your shins.'
common_errors.yanking_bar: Jerking the bar off the floor with a sudden pull rather than gradually pulling the slack out of the bar first — fails to build full-body tension before load is applied, increases bicep tear risk, and reduces total force production. Cue: 'pull the slack out, then press the floor away.'

common_errors.hip_flexion: Letting the hips sag into flexion rather than maintaining a neutral extended hip position throughout the hold. Hip flexion shortens the adductors and reduces their loading, converting a highly effective adductor strength exercise into a much less productive hip flexor and oblique drill.
common_errors.hip_rotation: Allowing the pelvis to rotate so the hips are no longer square to the floor. This is typically the pelvis dipping forward, which transfers load from the adductors and obliques into the lumbar extensors and defeats the intended bilateral hip-square position.
common_errors.wrong_lever_selection: Attempting a long-lever variation (foot on bench) before building adequate adductor strength with the short-lever (knee or mid-thigh on bench) version. The load on the adductor longus scales dramatically with lever arm length; premature progression is the primary mechanism for acute adductor strains during this exercise.
common_errors.bottom_leg_contact: Resting the lower leg on the floor rather than actively lifting it to create bilateral adductor loading. The bottom leg should be suspended beneath the bench, pressing against it from below; allowing it to rest on the ground eliminates its adductor contribution and halves the exercise's effectiveness.
common_errors.neck_tucking: Tilting the head forward or dropping the chin to the chest rather than maintaining neutral cervical alignment consistent with the side plank position. Though cosmetically minor, this disrupts the straight-line body position and is a reliable indicator of global fatigue that should prompt termination of the set.

common_errors.hip_rotation: Allowing the front hip to rotate externally or the rear hip to kick out during the descent — this collapses the sagittal plane intent of the lunge and removes the diagonal tension that specifically loads the gluteus medius and adductors; hips must stay squared to the front throughout.
common_errors.partial_range_of_motion: Only lowering a few inches rather than dropping until the front thigh approaches parallel to the floor — abbreviated reps reduce the eccentric gluteal and quad stimulus significantly and are usually a sign that hip mobility or motor control limitations need to be addressed.
common_errors.forward_trunk_lean: Allowing the torso to pitch excessively forward shifts load from the glutes and posterior chain to the lower back and reduces glute activation at the top of the movement, which is where the glutes should be at their highest demand.
common_errors.knee_valgus_on_front_leg: The front knee caving inward during the descent is a classic hip abductor weakness compensation — the gluteus medius of the front leg must maintain knee alignment over the second toe, making the curtsy lunge simultaneously a diagnostic and corrective tool for valgus collapse.
common_errors.instability_and_balance_rush: Moving too quickly through a movement that requires significant frontal-plane balance causes the athlete to stumble or compensate with the trunk — especially for beginners, practicing the static curtsy hold position before adding dynamic reps builds the pelvic stability required for safe loading.

common_errors.lumbar_arch: Allowing the lower back to lift off the floor as the arm or leg extends — the single most critical technical error. The entire purpose of the exercise is to brace the core to resist lumbar extension; once contact is lost, the exercise has failed and the spine is loaded passively rather than trained actively.
common_errors.rushing_reps: Moving through the arm-and-leg extension quickly using momentum rather than slow, deliberate neuromuscular control. The dead bug is a motor pattern drill first; speed eliminates the stabilization challenge that makes it effective and allows compensatory hip flexor dominance to mask core weakness.
common_errors.pelvic_tuck: Flattening the lumbar spine into posterior pelvic tilt as a coping strategy — a common instruction in yoga and Pilates settings but biomechanically incorrect. This is a cheat that substitutes passive posterior pelvic tilting for genuine anti-extension core engagement, and it trains the wrong motor pattern.
common_errors.same_side_limbs: Extending the arm and leg on the same side (ipsilateral) rather than opposite sides (contralateral). This eliminates the cross-body stabilization demand that makes the exercise neurologically challenging and reduces its carryover to athletic and functional movement.
common_errors.breath_holding: Holding the breath or breathing shallowly throughout the rep. Proper diaphragmatic breathing during the dead bug is integral to the intra-abdominal pressure mechanism that protects the lumbar spine; without it, the deep stabilizer co-contraction pattern is compromised.

common_errors.fully_passive_shoulders: Allowing the shoulders to rise completely to the ears with zero muscular tone. For general population and rehab use this is appropriate (spinal traction), but for shoulder stability training it removes all rotator cuff and scapular stabilizer demand and places the full load on passive capsular structures — problematic for those with any degree of shoulder hypermobility or instability.
common_errors.bent_elbows: Maintaining a slight bend in the elbows rather than fully extending the arms. Full elbow extension is required both for complete lat stretch and for the shoulder traction effect; partial extension means the biceps are bearing significant load eccentrically instead of the target tissues getting the intended stimulus.
common_errors.excessive_swinging: Generating pendulum-like body swing through uncontrolled mount or core disengagement. Swinging dissipates grip endurance rapidly and introduces shear forces at the shoulder; a light abdominal brace and controlled step-off will prevent it.
common_errors.breath_holding: Clenching the breath throughout the hold. Breath-holding dramatically accelerates grip failure and creates unnecessary intra-thoracic pressure; slow, controlled breathing allows the hang to be sustained far longer and the spine to decompress more fully.
common_errors.jumping_to_the_bar: Jumping and grabbing a high bar with momentum rather than stepping off a platform. Impact loading at the wrist, elbow, and glenohumeral joint without an established grip significantly increases the risk of ligament strain and an unsecured initial grip.

common_errors.bar_path_toward_neck: Lowering the bar toward the clavicles or throat rather than the lower chest creates dangerous shoulder joint stress and does not match the fiber direction of the costal and sternal pec heads, which are best loaded when the bar travels to the lower sternum.
common_errors.elbow_flare: Allowing the elbows to flare out to 90 degrees dramatically increases glenohumeral joint stress. Elite coaches cue a 45–60 degree elbow tuck, keeping the forearms stacked under the bar and maximizing safe force production.
common_errors.bouncing_bar_off_chest: Using momentum from a chest bounce removes the eccentric overload and can crack a rib under heavy loads. Controlled touch-and-go or a brief pause keeps muscle tension and reduces injury risk.
common_errors.inadequate_ankle_anchor: On a decline bench, unsecured feet will slide forward as fatigue accumulates, disrupting position and pulling the hips off the bench, which converts the decline into an arched flat press and eliminates the target angle.
common_errors.missing_the_unrack: Because the athlete's head is below the bar on a decline setup, unracking without a spotter or without pulling the bar to vertical first creates a severe risk of losing control of the bar above the face. Always have a spotter or use a power rack with safety pins set just above the chest.

common_errors.ground_contact_too_long: Spending more than 0.2 seconds on the ground after landing — Verkhoshansky's original specification was minimal amortization time to maximize the stretch-shortening cycle. Athletes who sink deeply into a squat before jumping up are essentially doing a squat jump from the bottom, not a reactive depth jump, and lose all SSC benefit.
common_errors.box_height_too_high: Dropping from an excessive height that exceeds the athlete's ability to absorb and redirect force — beyond the optimal range, longer ground contact times and reduced reactive strength index indicate the load is counterproductive and increases injury risk. Box height should be individualized to maximize jump height output.
common_errors.premature_use_without_strength_base: Introducing depth jumps to athletes who lack a 1.5x bodyweight squat or equivalent lower-body strength — the impact can be 3–4x bodyweight and undertrained musculotendinous tissue cannot safely absorb and redirect those forces, leading to acute or overuse injury.
common_errors.excessive_volume: Programming too many depth jumps per session or week — Verkhoshansky documented CNS fatigue and sleep disruption in athletes who overloaded this method. Depth jumps should be limited to 6–10 total contacts per session at most, 1–2 sessions per week, with adequate recovery.
common_errors.inconsistent_arm_swing: Not using a consistent arm swing pattern across reps — in training contexts, arm drive adds jump height and should be standardized per rep; in testing contexts (RSI measurement) arm position must be controlled to ensure valid comparisons across sessions.

common_errors.excessive_glenohumeral_extension: Allowing the elbows to travel far behind the torso at the bottom position so the shoulder joint passes into deep hyperextension — EMG and biomechanical research identifies this as the primary mechanism for pectoralis major tears at the musculotendinous junction, a catastrophic injury that has ended competitive careers; the humerus should not pass significantly behind the torso.
common_errors.depth_too_extreme: Dropping until the upper arms are below parallel without the requisite shoulder mobility or eccentric strength — going too deep dramatically increases anterior shoulder capsule stress and impingement risk, particularly in lifters with limited posterior shoulder mobility; the minimum safe depth cue is upper arm parallel to the floor.
common_errors.shrugging_at_top: Allowing the shoulders to elevate toward the ears at lockout rather than staying actively depressed — this shifts load onto the upper trapezius and away from the triceps and chest, and places the shoulder in a position of impingement risk particularly for overhead athletes.
common_errors.forward_lean_mismatch: Not intentionally controlling the degree of forward lean — a more upright torso preferentially recruits the triceps while a more pronounced forward lean shifts emphasis to the pectorals; when the lean is uncontrolled and variable between reps the muscular stimulus is inconsistent and injury risk increases.
common_errors.bodyweight_too_high_too_soon: Performing full bodyweight dips without the requisite baseline triceps and shoulder girdle strength — the dip is a significantly loaded exercise relative to body mass and beginners who cannot perform at least 5 controlled dips should use band assistance or a machine rather than performing poorly controlled reps that reinforce faulty mechanics.

common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: Arching the lower back to lift the leg higher rather than using pure hip extension — this is the most common error and fundamentally changes the exercise from a glute isolation to a lumbar extension movement. The spine should remain completely neutral; all movement occurs at the hip joint only.
common_errors.hip_rotation_and_tilt: The hip of the working leg externally rotating or the pelvis tilting to the opposite side during the kick — this substitution pattern recruits the hip flexors and TFL rather than the gluteus maximus. The hips must stay square to the floor throughout.
common_errors.leg_height_compensation: Lifting the leg as high as possible by compensating with spinal movement — more height does not mean more glute activation. Once the hip is in full extension, any further range comes from the lumbar spine. Stopping at parallel with the torso and squeezing the glute isometrically is more effective.
common_errors.using_momentum: Swinging the leg rapidly through the range of motion rather than performing a controlled, deliberate contraction — ballistic reps eliminate the time under tension that drives muscle adaptation and increase injury risk at the hip flexors on the return phase.
common_errors.supporting_knee_misalignment: The supporting knee migrating forward of the hip or the supporting hand drifting inward, destabilizing the base and causing compensatory torso movement. Both knees and both hands should maintain a stable four-point base throughout.
common_errors.not_flexing_knee_to_90_degrees: For the bent-knee variation, failing to maintain approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion causes the hamstrings to reach active insufficiency and take over from the glutes. The bent-knee cue is specifically designed to de-recruit the hamstrings and isolate the glute.

common_errors.bar_drifting_away_from_body: Allowing the barbell to move forward in an arc away from the torso during the curl rather than dragging it upward along the abdomen. The bar must physically contact or closely skim the body throughout the entire range of motion; this is what drives the elbows back into shoulder extension, which is the key mechanism that preferentially loads the biceps long head.
common_errors.elbow_not_traveling_behind_torso: Keeping the elbows at the sides (as in a standard curl) instead of driving them progressively behind the body as the bar rises. The posterior elbow travel is not a stylistic option — it is the anatomical mechanism that keeps the shoulder in extension and maximizes long-head stretch and supination advantage throughout the range of motion.
common_errors.excessive_shoulder_shrug: Elevating the shoulders at the top to get the bar higher. This is a compensation for using too much weight or an insufficient range of motion; it shifts load to the upper traps and anterior deltoid and is an early indicator that the load should be reduced.
common_errors.wrist_breakdown: Allowing the wrists to flex backward (extend) under load, which partially unloads the biceps and increases strain on the wrist flexors and extensor tendons. The wrists should remain neutral throughout — if they are collapsing, the load is too heavy for the current wrist and forearm strength.

common_errors.dumbbells_too_far_apart_at_bottom: Allowing the dumbbells to drop excessively wide at the bottom so the elbows pass behind the torso — this places the pec tendons and anterior capsule under extreme stretch stress, a common cause of pectoral tears, and is more dangerous with dumbbells than a barbell because there is no bar to limit the range.
common_errors.uncontrolled_descent: Letting the dumbbells fall quickly rather than lowering under muscular control — the eccentric phase is where significant hypertrophic stimulus occurs, and uncontrolled descent also increases the risk of the joint being forced into an impingement position.
common_errors.bringing_dumbbells_together_at_top: Clinking the dumbbells together at lockout — this unloads the pecs at the peak contraction point and transfers force to the wrists; keeping a slight gap maintains tension through the full range.
common_errors.neutral_grip_loss: Allowing the wrists to rotate so palms face fully toward the feet rather than slightly inward or neutral — a slight neutral or semi-supinated grip reduces bicipital tendon impingement and keeps the shoulder in a safer alignment, particularly important given the unconstrained range of dumbbells.
common_errors.asymmetrical_pressing: One arm pressing faster or further than the other, which often reveals a bilateral strength imbalance that will worsen over time if not addressed directly — coaches should film from the foot of the bench to catch side-to-side discrepancies.

common_errors.no_supination: Many lifters perform the dumbbell curl without rotating the forearm into full supination at the top — this deprives the biceps of its secondary function as a supinator and reduces peak contraction. The palm should rotate fully upward during the concentric phase.
common_errors.elbow_drift_and_shoulder_flexion: Allowing the elbow to swing forward uses the anterior deltoid to cheat the weight past the sticking point rather than relying solely on elbow flexion. The upper arm should remain perpendicular to the floor and locked to the side throughout.
common_errors.asymmetry_between_sides: Alternating curls frequently allow the weaker side to receive less time under tension or a shorter ROM as fatigue accumulates. Coaches flag this as a bilateral deficit that, left uncorrected, compounds over time into visible arm size differences.
common_errors.incomplete_elbow_extension: Stopping short of full elbow extension at the bottom eliminates the loaded stretch on the biceps long head, which evidence suggests is one of the primary stimuli for long-head hypertrophy. Arms should return to a fully extended position each rep.
common_errors.excessive_torso_sway: Rocking the torso backward with each rep substitutes lumbar momentum for biceps strength. Unlike the barbell curl where slight backward lean is sometimes cued, the dumbbell curl should be performed with the torso rigid and neutral.

common_errors.excessive_elbow_extension: Straightening the arms near full extension dramatically increases the torque at the shoulder joint at its weakest position (arms abducted and horizontal), which is a primary mechanism of pec major proximal tears. The elbows must maintain a consistent 10–20 degree soft bend throughout the entire arc.
common_errors.lowering_too_far_past_parallel: Lowering the dumbbells well below the plane of the bench — especially under heavy loads — places extreme stretch tension on the anterior capsule and increases pec tendon injury risk. The arms should descend to roughly parallel with the bench, or slightly below if shoulder health permits, then immediately reverse.
common_errors.treating_it_as_a_press: Bending the elbows during the concentric and pushing in a pressing pattern rather than squeezing the pecs through horizontal adduction removes almost all isolation benefit. The movement should feel like closing a wide hug, not pressing the ceiling.
common_errors.load_too_heavy: Heavier weights inevitably cause elbow bending, range-of-motion compensation, and dangerous shoulder stress at the bottom. The dumbbell fly is an isolation movement best performed in moderate-to-high rep ranges with loads that permit full control of the arc, not a max-effort movement.
common_errors.lack_of_scapular_depression: Allowing the shoulder blades to ride up and anteriorly tilt as the arms open reduces the stable base from which the pectorals can generate force and exposes the rotator cuff to impingement stress. Pulling the shoulder blades down and back before each rep and maintaining that retraction protects the joint and improves muscle activation.

common_errors.excessive_knee_dip: Dipping into a quarter squat or deeper wastes time and energy on the dip-and-drive, and converts the push press into a partial thruster. The dip should be a brief, shallow knee bend (approximately 10–20 degrees) that loads the quads and glutes for an immediate explosive reversal, not a controlled descent.
common_errors.forward_trunk_lean_during_dip: Allowing the torso to angle forward during the dip causes the drive to project the dumbbells forward rather than vertically, resulting in a horizontal momentum component that must be corrected midair. The torso stays vertical throughout, with the hips moving straight down.
common_errors.rebending_knees_during_press: Bending the knees again as the dumbbells pass the sticking point is a missed-rep fault borrowed from the push jerk. In the push press, the legs extend fully and lock out before the arms complete the press; a second dip is never used.
common_errors.dumbbells_not_in_proper_front_rack: Starting with the dumbbells resting loosely at the shoulders with palms forward — as in a strict press — misses the neutral-grip 'rack' position that keeps the wrists stacked over the elbows and allows the drive to transfer directly into the dumbbells. A neutral grip with the dumbbells lightly braced on the anterior deltoids is the optimal position.
common_errors.pressing_only_with_arms: Initiating the press with the arms before the legs have completed their drive disconnects the kinetic chain and reduces the load the athlete can handle, defeating the primary purpose of the push press. The leg drive should be complete before the arms take over, creating a seamless force handoff.

common_errors.sitting_too_upright_without_back_support: Performing seated dumbbell presses on a flat bench without incline back support forces the lifter to stabilize the torso independently — without a backrest set to 90° this often causes the torso to lean back excessively, converting a shoulder press into a partial incline press and reducing deltoid isolation.
common_errors.dumbbells_drifting_forward_at_top: Allowing the dumbbells to drift forward in front of the head at lockout instead of directly overhead — this shortens the pressing range, reduces anterior deltoid peak contraction, and shifts the movement toward an incline press pattern rather than true vertical pressing.
common_errors.asymmetrical_lockout: One arm reaching full extension while the other lags — this asymmetry is often masked by the body tilting toward the weaker side and should be caught early because it will compound a bilateral strength imbalance if left uncorrected.
common_errors.elbows_flaring_behind_the_body: Starting with the upper arms too far behind the plane of the torso (elbows behind the ears) rather than in the scapular plane — this position internally rotates the shoulder into impingement risk under load and should be corrected by having elbows slightly forward of the torso at the bottom position.

common_errors.pulling_to_chin_instead_of_face: Targeting the pull to chin or neck height rather than toward the forehead or upper face — lower pull height converts the movement into a horizontal row that biases the lats and mid-traps, completely removing the posterior deltoid and rotator cuff recruitment that is the entire purpose of the exercise.
common_errors.elbows_pointing_down: Allowing the elbows to drop toward the floor during the pull rather than maintaining them parallel to the floor or slightly above — elbow position dictates which muscles are recruited. Elbows up and out creates the horizontal abduction pattern that loads the posterior delt and rotator cuff; elbows down creates a row pattern.
common_errors.omitting_external_rotation: Pulling the rope to the face but not following through with shoulder external rotation at the end range — the final movement of rotating the hands back and out (thumbs pointing behind the athlete) is what maximally activates the infraspinatus and teres minor. Without it, rotator cuff training stimulus is minimal.
common_errors.excessive_load_compromising_form: Using weight that forces the athlete to lean back, use momentum, or lose elbow position — face pulls are a high-rep shoulder health exercise and should be trained with loads that permit perfect mechanics through every rep. Form breakdown under load is counterproductive in an exercise prescribed specifically for joint health.
common_errors.inconsistent_cable_height: Setting the cable at shoulder height or below rather than at or above forehead level — the cable angle must be downward toward the face from above to create the correct vector for posterior deltoid and rotator cuff loading. A low cable changes the force vector and muscle recruitment profile substantially.

common_errors.shrugging_shoulders: Allowing the shoulders to elevate or roll forward under load rather than packing the scapulae down and back — this transfers stress away from the mid and lower traps and onto the neck, increasing injury risk and reducing the postural benefit that makes carries valuable.
common_errors.excessive_lean: Tilting the torso to one side or leaning excessively forward, which shifts load onto passive spinal structures rather than the stabilizing musculature. Coaches look for ears, shoulders, and hips stacked vertically throughout the walk.
common_errors.overstriding: Taking long, slow steps rather than short, controlled strides — long strides create greater lateral trunk sway, destabilize the carry, and reduce time under tension for the postural muscles that are the primary training target.
common_errors.grip_failure_ignored: Continuing to walk when the weights are visibly rolling out of the fingers rather than resetting or terminating the set. Once grip fails, the traps and upper back lose the tension needed to maintain position and the training stimulus collapses.
common_errors.breath_holding_entire_set: Fully bracing and apnea-breathing the way one would in a squat or deadlift is unsustainable for loaded carry distances. Athletes should learn rhythmic bracing with each step — inhale, brace, step, step; re-brace on the next breath — to sustain intra-abdominal pressure without accumulating excessive CO2 debt.

aliases: quadruped hip abduction with external rotation

common_errors.torso_rotation_and_hip_hiking: Rotating the pelvis and trunk toward the lifting leg or hiking the opposite hip to assist the lift — this collapses the quadruped spinal position and substitutes lumbar lateral flexion for true hip abduction/external rotation, removing the glute from its working range.
common_errors.wrist_and_shoulder_collapse: Allowing the weight-bearing arm and shoulder on the working side to sink or internally rotate, which destabilizes the entire quadruped base and reduces the spine's ability to remain neutral — scapular and wrist stability must be maintained actively.
common_errors.knee_below_90_degrees: Failing to maintain the knee at or near 90 degrees throughout the movement reduces the hip external rotation challenge; the bent knee position is what makes fire hydrants distinctive from straight-leg abduction by combining ER with abduction.
common_errors.swinging_for_height: Prioritizing how high the knee can go rather than keeping the movement controlled and within a neutral pelvic position — leg height above hip level is only achievable with pelvic compensation, so quality beats height every time.
common_errors.no_progressive_overload: Performing fire hydrants bodyweight indefinitely without adding a band or ankle weight — as a bodyweight exercise, EMG activation is relatively low, and adding even light resistance (small loop band above knees) meaningfully increases gluteal demand to a therapeutic and training-effective range.

common_errors.bouncing_elbows_off_floor: Allowing the elbows to slam into the ground and using the rebound to initiate the press creates a ballistic force spike at the shoulder and eliminates the entire advantage of the pause. Elbows should touch down with control and pause with full muscle tension maintained before the concentric.
common_errors.losing_scapular_retraction: Allowing the shoulder blades to protract at the top of the rep (chasing maximum extension) jams the acromioclavicular joint and reduces the stable base needed for safe pressing. Keeping the scapulae retracted and depressed throughout preserves both shoulder health and pressing mechanics.
common_errors.hips_rising_off_floor: Bridging the hips off the ground to generate momentum fundamentally changes the mechanics, increasing range of motion and allowing the lower body to assist — which defeats the purpose of the floor press as a controlled partial-range tricep and lockout drill.
common_errors.excessive_arm_extension_at_top: Overextending and locking out with force creates joint impact at the elbow. The lockout should be controlled and firm, not a sudden snapping movement, particularly under heavy barbell loads.
common_errors.incorrect_setup_without_rack: Rolling a loaded barbell from the floor to the pressing position without a spotter or rack is a common injury mechanism. Using a power rack with safeties set at floor level, or cleaning dumbbells from the knees, is always the preferred setup method.

common_errors.using_too_much_weight: Loading the front raise heavier than the anterior deltoid can control — because the front delt is already heavily recruited by every pressing movement, excessive loading causes lifters to recruit the upper trapezius, core, and lower back through momentum, completely defeating the isolation purpose and risking impingement.
common_errors.body_swing_momentum: Rocking the torso backward to initiate the movement rather than moving only the arms — this transfers the work from the anterior deltoid to the spinal erectors and lower back, particularly dangerous because the loaded moment arm at L5-S1 with arms extended in front of the body is large even with light dumbbells.
common_errors.raising_too_high: Lifting the arms above parallel (shoulder height) or approaching vertical — above 90° flexion the supraspinatus tendon enters the coracoacromial impingement zone, and given how much indirect anterior delt work accumulates from pressing, adding this stress through excessive front raise height is a common source of chronic shoulder pathology.
common_errors.shoulder_shrugging: Allowing the shoulder girdle to elevate and shrug upward as the arms rise — this transfers work to the upper trapezius rather than the anterior deltoid and is a sign the load is too heavy or the lifter lacks body awareness; the coaching cue is to keep shoulders down and away from the ears throughout.
common_errors.insufficient_bracing: Performing front raises without a stable, braced core — because the weight acts directly in front of the body at arm's length, even moderate loads create a large forward flexion moment at the lumbar spine, causing lifters with a loose core to compensate with lumbar hyperextension and spinal shear loading.

common_errors.elbows_dropping: The elbows falling below bar level during the descent shifts the bar forward off the shelf of the deltoids and forces the wrists to bear the load — this almost always results in the torso collapsing forward, completely defeating the upright positioning that makes the front squat superior for quad development. The single highest-leverage cue in the lift is 'drive elbows up and forward' at all times.
common_errors.excessive_forward_lean: The torso pitching forward as the lifter exits the bottom position is often confused with 'normal' squat mechanics but in the front squat it signals inadequate quad strength, insufficient ankle dorsiflexion, or a core that cannot maintain intra-abdominal pressure under load. It places the bar far in front of the midfoot and makes the lift mechanically impossible to complete at heavy loads.
common_errors.valgus_knee_collapse: The knees caving inward — particularly under fatigue or at heavy loads — introduces lateral shear forces across the knee joint that accumulate into injury over time. It usually reflects a combination of hip abductor weakness, insufficient hip external rotation from the setup, or a stance that is too wide for the lifter's hip anatomy.
common_errors.heels_rising: The heels coming off the floor indicates insufficient ankle dorsiflexion and forces the lifter onto the forefoot, compromising balance and shifting the knee stress pattern.
