Elevating the heels on small plates or weightlifting shoes is a legitimate loading strategy; uncontrolled heel rise is not.
common_errors.grip_too_tight_wrists: Gripping the bar with a fully closed fist during a clean-grip setup forces the wrists into painful extension and is the primary cause of front squat wrist pain. The bar rests on the front deltoid shelf — the fingers are merely guides. Releasing the pinky and ring fingers while maintaining high elbows relieves the wrist angle without compromising bar security.

common_errors.spinal_flexion_instead_of_hip_hinge: Rounding the thoracic and lumbar spine on the descent rather than hinging purely at the hip — on the GHD, athletes have ample range to fall into spinal flexion, which is distinct from the intended hip flexion. Spinal flexion under load is a primary mechanism of disc injury.
common_errors.hyperextending_at_top: Arching the lower back excessively at the top of the movement beyond neutral — the GHD's high range of motion makes this especially easy to do. The finish position should align the torso with the upper legs, not bow past it.
common_errors.not_using_full_range: Stopping short of a full hip hinge at the bottom of the movement, reducing the hamstring and glute stretch that creates the training stimulus. Athletes should allow the torso to lower until the hip flexion is near its full range while maintaining neutral spine.
common_errors.cervical_hyperextension: Looking upward or craning the neck backward throughout the movement, placing sustained load on the cervical spine in extension. The head should remain in neutral, consistent with the thoracic spine position.
common_errors.inadequate_pad_height: Setting the hip pad too high or too low — too high pinches at the hip and limits ROM, too low shifts the pivot point toward the lower lumbar region, converting the movement into a spinal exercise rather than a hip hinge.

common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: Arching the lower back at the top of the movement instead of achieving true hip extension — the pelvis should posteriorly tilt slightly at lockout, not the spine hyperextend. This shifts load from the glutes to the erector spinae and increases compressive stress on the lumbar vertebrae.
common_errors.hamstring_dominance: Placing feet too far from the hips causes the hamstrings to dominate the movement rather than the glutes, often resulting in cramping in the posterior thigh. Feet should be close enough that the shins are roughly vertical at the top position.
common_errors.losing_glute_activation: Rushing through reps without consciously squeezing the glutes at the top — the glutes are prone to inhibition and this exercise demands deliberate contraction. Athletes who just 'lift their hips' rather than 'squeeze their glutes' consistently show lower EMG activation.
common_errors.hip_asymmetry: One hip rising higher than the other, revealing a unilateral glute or hip flexor imbalance. Left uncorrected, this asymmetry transfers load to the stronger side and reinforces the imbalance over time.
common_errors.rib_flare: The ribcage lifting off the floor or chest puffing up as the hips rise — a sign of lost core bracing and spinal neutrality. Cue the athlete to keep their ribs 'heavy' and maintain a slight posterior pelvic tilt throughout.
common_errors.toe_pushing: Driving through the toes rather than the heels significantly reduces gluteus maximus activation and shifts load to the quads. Heels should be the primary contact point with the floor.

common_errors.forward_lean: The torso tipping forward as the lifter descends is the most common error and entirely negates the goblet squat's primary teaching value — the front-loaded counterbalance that produces an upright chest. It usually indicates inadequate core bracing or a lifter who is initiating the movement by pushing the hips back rather than sitting down between the feet.
common_errors.elbows_contacting_thighs: The elbows crashing into the inner thighs at the bottom is often treated as a depth cue, but using them to pry the knees out creates a load transfer to the upper body and removes tension from the quads and glutes entirely. The elbows can make light contact as a mobility check but should not be bearing weight.
common_errors.heels_rising: The heels coming off the floor cuts the squat depth short and forces undue load onto the forefoot and knee. The goblet squat is specifically suited to teaching full-range squatting with a neutral ankle; if heels rise consistently, the primary culprit is limited ankle dorsiflexion requiring targeted mobility work.
common_errors.weight_drifting_from_chest: Allowing the weight to drift away from the body as the lifter descends extends the moment arm and dramatically increases the demand on the lower back, turning a quad-dominant movement into a lower back stressor. The weight should stay pressed against the sternum throughout the entire range of motion.
common_errors.shallow_depth: Stopping well above parallel eliminates the primary reasons to prescribe the goblet squat — full hip flexion for mobility development and the deep-range quad stimulus. Unless depth is limited by injury or genuine mobility restriction, coaches should cue the athlete to sit until the hip crease drops below the top of the knee.

common_errors.rounding_the_lower_back: Allowing the lumbar spine to flex during the hinge transforms the exercise from a powerful posterior chain strengthener into one of the highest-risk movements in the weight room — the bar position on the upper back creates an enormous flexion moment that can acutely injure intervertebral discs. The lumbar must maintain its natural arch throughout; if the back rounds at any load, the weight is too heavy.
common_errors.excessive_load: Good mornings are routinely and dangerously overloaded because the movement resembles a squat setup and lifters benchmark loading against their squat. Elite coaches cap good mornings at 30–60% of a lifter's back squat max for most purposes; going heavier demands a level of posterior chain bracing and technique mastery that takes years to develop safely.
common_errors.locking_the_knees: Performing the movement with completely rigid, locked knees places the entire hamstring load on the distal insertion near the knee rather than distributing it across the full muscle belly. A slight but deliberate knee bend allows the hamstrings to pull from optimal length and protects the posterior knee structures.
common_errors.bar_placement_too_low: Dropping the bar below the traps into a low-bar position significantly increases the moment arm and the stress on the lumbar spine at bottom position — without the corresponding quad loading that justifies low-bar in the squat. Good mornings should be executed from a high-bar or mid-trap position to keep the fulcrum mechanics manageable.
common_errors.insufficient_hip_hinge: Squatting down rather than hinging back at the hips — a common beginner pattern — defeats the purpose of the exercise and minimizes the eccentric hamstring and erector stretch. The hips must travel backward as the torso travels forward, maintaining a consistent shin angle throughout the movement.

common_errors.swinging_the_dumbbell: Using body momentum to assist the lift shifts the load away from the brachialis and brachioradialis — the very muscles hammer curls are designed to isolate. Because the brachialis is not a supinator, it cannot compensate with rotation, so momentum directly steals from its workload.
common_errors.grip_rolling_to_fingertips: Allowing the dumbbell to roll toward the fingers as fatigue sets in prevents full elbow lockout at the top, reducing the brachioradialis's range of active contraction. The dumbbell should stay firmly anchored in the palm with a stacked fist-over-wrist position.
common_errors.partial_range_of_motion: Stopping the curl before full elbow extension at the bottom and before peak flexion at the top shortens the brachialis through a reduced ROM — problematic because the brachialis is a pure elbow flexor with no supination function to compensate.
common_errors.elbow_flare: Allowing the elbows to splay outward during the curl reduces the mechanical efficiency of elbow flexion and can place the lateral elbow structures under shear stress. Elbows should track close to the torso throughout the movement.
common_errors.excessive_wrist_deviation: Cocking the wrist into ulnar or radial deviation during the curl stresses the wrist extensor tendons and takes loading off the target muscles. The wrist should stay neutral with the forearm throughout all phases of the movement.

common_errors.quad_dominant_setup: Pushing the knees forward into the hang rather than driving the hips back loads the quadriceps instead of the hamstrings, removing the elastic pre-stretch of the posterior chain that generates the explosive hip drive; athletes should hinge like a Romanian deadlift to reach the hang position.
common_errors.early_arm_pull: Attempting to muscle the bar up by bending the elbows before full triple extension — because the hang position shortens the range of motion, athletes mistakenly compensate with arm strength rather than patient hip drive, which caps how much weight can ever be successfully cleaned.
common_errors.passive_lat_engagement: Letting the upper back go slack during the descent into the hang causes the bar to drift forward from the body, lengthening the moment arm and creating a forward-swinging bar path that makes the front rack catch position nearly unreachable.
common_errors.rushing_the_hang_position: Rapidly bouncing through the hang position without controlling the descent removes the stretch-shortening cycle benefit and causes athletes to initiate from an inconsistent position on every rep, producing erratic bar paths and inconsistent catches.
common_errors.low_receiving_elbows: Catching the bar with the elbows pointing downward rather than driving them aggressively forward and upward allows the bar to roll off the front rack and onto the wrists, creating wrist pain and limiting how much weight can be received safely.

common_errors.quad_dominant_hang_position: Letting the quads push the bar forward as the lifter lowers into the hang rather than loading the hamstrings by driving the hips back; this kills posterior chain tension and forces the lifter to rely on arms rather than leg drive to initiate the pull.
common_errors.bar_drifting_forward: Allowing the bar to swing away from the body during the pull collapses the lifter's balance toward the toes and makes it nearly impossible to achieve a clean front rack — the elbows should drive 'up and out' to keep the bar close throughout.
common_errors.early_arm_bend: Bending the elbows before full hip and knee extension is reached; because the hang position shortens the range of motion, athletes often compensate by trying to muscle the bar up with their arms rather than waiting for hip explosion to do the work.
common_errors.rushing_the_drop: Hurrying the descent into the hang position in cycling sets causes the athlete to reach the hang without any loaded hamstring tension, turning the powerful elastic rebound of the posterior chain into a passive sag and greatly reducing power output.
common_errors.excessive_foot_width_at_catch: Landing with the feet significantly wider than the squat stance on each rep indicates the lifter is jumping out to the sides to lower the bar to a catchable height rather than actively pulling under it, which masks a deficiency in rate of force development.

common_errors.hip_flexor_dominance: Simply swinging the legs upward through hip flexion without the critical posterior pelvic tilt that brings the rectus abdominis into the movement. Without cueing the pelvis to posteriorly tilt and the lower abs to actively curl toward the chest, the exercise becomes almost exclusively a hip flexor strengthener with minimal abdominal activation.
common_errors.swinging_and_momentum: Using body swing or kipping momentum to complete reps rather than controlling the lift under muscular tension. This is particularly problematic in the descent phase — the eccentric lowering is where most of the abdominal training value lies, and momentum bypasses it entirely.
common_errors.limited_range: Stopping at hip height (90 degrees) when greater strength and flexibility permit a fuller range. Taking the legs through a larger arc, approaching toes-to-bar, dramatically increases the rectus abdominis demand and distinguishes genuine strength from a truncated exercise.
common_errors.shoulder_elevation: Allowing the shoulders to shrug upward toward the ears rather than actively depressing and retracting the scapulae before and throughout the movement. Proper shoulder packing creates a stable base and protects the glenohumeral joint under the load of repeated hanging repetitions.
common_errors.early_progression: Advancing to straight-leg or toes-to-bar variations before mastering controlled bent-knee raises, which is a predictable path to low back injury. The straight-leg version creates substantially greater lumbar shear force; it should only be used when the bent-knee version can be executed with a full, deliberate posterior pelvic tilt.

common_errors.angle_too_steep: Setting the bench at 45° or higher — EMG research shows that inclinations above 30–40° dramatically shift primary activation from the clavicular pectoralis to the anterior deltoid, effectively turning the exercise into a shoulder press with a bench; the optimal incline for clavicular pec emphasis is 30°.
common_errors.bar_touching_neck_rather_than_upper_ches: Allowing the bar to drift high and touch near the clavicles or throat instead of the upper sternum — the correct contact point is the upper chest, and bringing the bar to the neck places dangerous compressive load on the cervical structures and reduces the pectoral stretch needed for muscle development.
common_errors.scapular_instability: Failing to retract and depress the scapulae before pressing — this is more critical on the incline than the flat bench because the steeper angle is inherently more destabilizing to the shoulder girdle, and without a packed scapular position the glenohumeral joint lacks the mechanical foundation needed for safe loading.
common_errors.elbows_flaring_perpendicular: Allowing elbows to flare out to 90° relative to the torso — at an incline this combination of abduction and extension under load significantly increases anterior shoulder impingement and pec minor strain; elbows should stay at 45–75° of flare.
common_errors.excessive_weight_relative_to_flat: Loading the incline to the same percentage of 1RM as the flat bench — most lifters are 10–30% weaker on the incline due to the reduced contribution from the larger sternocostal pec, and overloading leads to compensatory motion, elbow flare, and loss of back position.

common_errors.wrong_bench_angle: Setting the bench too upright (above 60°) or too flat (below 30°). Research shows that approximately 45–60° elbow extension places the biceps in the maximum length-tension stretch at the start of the rep; too upright reduces the shoulder extension and negates the pre-stretch advantage; too flat causes the weight to swing forward during the rep.
common_errors.shoulder_flexion_compensation: Swinging the upper arm forward at the beginning of the rep to generate momentum, negating the passive pre-stretch that makes this curl superior to standing curls. The upper arm must remain hanging passively behind the torso throughout the movement — the shoulder stays in extension.
common_errors.not_fully_extending_at_bottom: Stopping the descent before the elbow reaches full extension. The key mechanism of the incline curl is that the long head is trained at maximal length, which research identifies as particularly potent for hypertrophy; partial range-of-motion at the bottom eliminates this advantage.
common_errors.too_heavy_a_load: Selecting the same weight as standing curls. The incline position removes the ability to body-swing and increases the passive stretch under load, making it considerably harder; most lifters should use 15–25% less weight than a standing curl to maintain controlled form throughout the full range of motion.

common_errors.bench_angle_too_steep: Setting the bench above 45 degrees shifts the primary load from the clavicular pecs to the anterior deltoids, turning a chest exercise into essentially a shoulder press. EMG data shows maximal upper pec activation occurs around 30–44 degrees; anything steeper than 60 degrees has the delts dominating.
common_errors.dumbbells_resting_on_shoulders: Allowing the dumbbells to rest against the shoulders at the bottom rather than maintaining tension reduces time under tension and eliminates the stretch stimulus on the clavicular fibers. The dumbbells should stop near chest level with the pecs loaded, not deposited.
common_errors.elbows_flared_perpendicular: Letting the elbows flare out to 90 degrees at the bottom places maximum shear force on the shoulder joint in its most vulnerable position. A 45–75 degree elbow tuck keeps the rotator cuff safe while maintaining pec recruitment.
common_errors.scooping_with_lower_back: Excessive lumbar hyperextension to generate momentum or hit the lockout effectively converts the incline press into a decline press, defeating the purpose of the angle and placing compressive load on the lumbar spine.
common_errors.dumbbells_colliding_at_top: Banging the dumbbells together at the top of each rep unloads the chest at peak contraction and risks destabilizing the shoulder. Stopping just short of contact maintains constant tension on the target muscles.

common_errors.excessive_load: Using too heavy a load shifts the stimulus from power development to strength endurance — research consistently shows peak power output occurs at 0–40% of 1RM depending on training status. Heavy loads force the athlete to decelerate through the top of the movement, defeating the ballistic intent.
common_errors.stiff_landing: Landing with rigid joints rather than absorbing through an immediate countermovement — the most effective programming uses the landing as the loading phase for the next rep (reactive jump squat), and athletes who land stiffly both increase injury risk and halve the SSC contribution.
common_errors.forward_torso_collapse: The torso pitching aggressively forward during the descent or jump phase — in loaded variations this dramatically increases lumbar flexion moment and can cause disc stress. The chest should stay up throughout the movement.
common_errors.shallow_countermovement: Never descending to at least a quarter squat before jumping — athletes who only dip minimally never train the full hip extension range critical for acceleration and vertical power production, and the SSC contribution is minimal.
common_errors.loss_of_maximal_intent: Treating later reps as 'just getting through the set' rather than maximal explosive effort on every rep — jump squats are a CNS-intensive power exercise where submaximal effort provides minimal power adaptation. The moment jump height visibly drops, the set should end.

common_errors.squat_pattern_substitution: Using the knees to drive the movement rather than explosive hip extension — the swing is a hip hinge, not a squat. When athletes squat-swing, the quads take over, the posterior chain disengages, and the explosive hip snap that defines the movement disappears. The knees should bend minimally during the hike.
common_errors.arm_lifting: Using shoulder flexion to raise the kettlebell rather than letting hip drive propel it — the arms should be passive connectors transmitting force from the hips, not prime movers. If the kettlebell goes up because of shoulder effort, the exercise loses its conditioning and posterior chain stimulus.
common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension_at_top: Leaning back at the top of the swing instead of achieving a vertical standing plank position — the finish position should be full hip extension with glutes squeezed and a tall, vertical torso. Hyperextension compresses lumbar vertebrae and is a common cause of lower back pain from swings.
common_errors.passive_hike: Letting the kettlebell drift backward passively instead of actively hiking it between the legs to create pre-stretch tension in the hamstrings. The hike should be aggressive — actively pulling the bell back to load the posterior chain before the hip drive.
common_errors.neck_position: Looking up throughout the movement, extending the cervical spine — the neck should remain in neutral, following the natural curve of the spine. Sustained cervical hyperextension under load causes neck fatigue and can contribute to upper cervical dysfunction.
common_errors.losing_lat_engagement: Failing to pack the lats and maintain tension in the shoulder girdle — without lat engagement the shoulder is unsupported at end-range, increasing impingement risk. Cue: 'bend the handle' or 'protect your armpits.'

common_errors.pressing_across_body: Driving the bar diagonally across the midline rather than straight forward along the shoulder's sagittal plane reduces force transfer efficiency and creates unnecessary rotational torque on the lumbar spine. The elbow and shoulder should stack with the bar traveling straight out from the socket.
common_errors.hips_forward_lean: In kneeling variations, allowing the hips to shift forward into hip flexion reduces core anti-extension demand and compresses the lumbar spine. Coaches cue a posterior pelvic tilt and a squeezed glute on the down knee to maintain neutral spine.
common_errors.grip_at_the_sleeve: Grabbing the bare barbell sleeve without a plate or landmine handle forces the wrist into an unstable position and creates sharp pain in the wrist joint under load. A small plate on the end or a proper handle attachment provides necessary wrist support.
common_errors.bar_path_going_overhead: Trying to press the bar to full vertical overhead rather than to the natural endpoint of the arc puts the shoulder into impingement-risk territory and is biomechanically impossible with a pivoting landmine. The endpoint is in front of and above the shoulder, roughly 45 degrees, not straight overhead.
common_errors.insufficient_core_bracing: In the standing or split-stance variation, failing to brace the core before pressing causes visible lateral flexion as the load is applied unilaterally. This compensatory lean shifts load to the lumbar stabilizers, negating the anti-lateral-flexion benefit and risking low back strain.

common_errors.excessive_posterior_lean: Leaning far back during the pull until the movement becomes closer to an incline row than a vertical pulldown — this shifts emphasis away from the vertical lat-shortening function and reduces the exercise's specificity for the pull-up pattern it is commonly used to develop.
common_errors.behind_the_neck_execution: Pulling the bar behind the head to the base of the skull rather than to the clavicle and upper sternum in front — behind-neck pulldowns place the cervical spine in forced flexion and the glenohumeral joint at near-maximal external rotation under load, with a high risk of cervical and rotator cuff injury and no demonstrated activation advantage.
common_errors.scapular_elevation_throughout: Allowing the shoulders to rise toward the ears rather than actively depressing and retracting the scapulae as the bar descends — identical mechanics to the pull-up error; without scapular depression, the upper trapezius and neck dominate instead of the lats.
common_errors.grip_width_misbelief: Defaulting to the widest grip possible under the assumption it maximizes lat width — EMG research does not support meaningful lat activation differences between grip widths. Excessively wide grip reduces range of motion, places greater wrist and shoulder stress, and reduces the load an athlete can use.
common_errors.not_pausing_at_full_contraction: Bouncing the bar off the chest or sternum at the bottom rather than briefly pausing with the bar touching and scapulae fully retracted and depressed — the pause eliminates momentum, confirms full lat shortening, and is the difference between training the lat through its full range versus only its stretched position.

common_errors.knee_band_placement: Placing the band above the knees rather than at the ankles or feet significantly reduces gluteus medius activation — research shows ankle/foot band placement generates higher GMed activity (up to 50% MVIC) and lower TFL recruitment than knee placement, making it the preferred position for hip abductor targeting.
common_errors.upright_posture_instead_of_minisquat: Performing the exercise while standing fully upright rather than in a slight hip-and-knee-flexed mini-squat position reduces gluteus medius activation; the 30-degree hip/knee flexion position preferentially loads GMed over TFL and is the evidence-backed technique recommendation.
common_errors.leading_with_the_weak_side: Stepping with the weaker hip leading — EMG data shows the stance leg (trailing leg) generates significantly higher gluteus medius activation (36–50% MVIC) than the moving leg (19–33% MVIC), so clinicians should cue patients to step away from, not toward, the weak side.
common_errors.overstriding: Taking steps too large for the available hip abductor strength forces the pelvis to drop and the trunk to sway, which substitutes lumbar lateral flexion for true abduction — steps should be short and controlled to maintain pelvic neutral throughout.
common_errors.bilateral_direction_error: Performing equal steps in both directions simultaneously without recognizing the asymmetric intent of the exercise — for rehabilitation of hip abductor weakness, evidence suggests stepping laterally away from the affected side is more targeted and therapeutically appropriate.

common_errors.too_small_a_bound: Taking small hops rather than maximal lateral leaps — the exercise's value comes from peak lateral force production and single-leg landing absorption; minimal bounds train neither quality effectively and reduce the power stimulus to near zero.
common_errors.knee_valgus_on_landing: Landing with valgus collapse of the stance knee — the glute medius must fire rapidly to control the knee in a neutral position over the second toe. Knee cave on landing significantly increases ACL and medial knee stress and should be corrected before increasing distance.
common_errors.poor_landing_stability: Hopping immediately off the landing foot without absorbing and controlling the touchdown — the single-leg landing demands eccentric deceleration before the next push. Athletes who can't stick a landing for 1–2 seconds before rebounding lack the unilateral stability to safely perform high-speed bounding.
common_errors.asymmetrical_distance: Bounding farther to one side than the other — often reflects a unilateral strength or stability deficit that is worth identifying and addressing directly, particularly in athletes returning from lower-limb injury.
common_errors.hip_hinge_lost: Losing a slight forward hip hinge during push-off, reducing the contribution of the glute and hamstring in propulsion — the movement should initiate from hip extension, not just knee extension, to ensure the posterior chain drives the bound.

common_errors.knee_over_toe_collapse: Allowing the stepping knee to travel well past the toes or cave inward in the frontal plane during the lateral descent — the knee should track directly over the second toe and stay in vertical alignment with the shin; valgus collapse here specifically indicates gluteus medius weakness and can stress the medial knee structures.
common_errors.insufficient_step_width: Taking too small a lateral step limits hip abduction range and shifts the movement into more of a sumo squat, reducing the adductor lengthening stimulus that makes the lateral lunge distinct — a sufficiently wide step should produce noticeable inner thigh stretch at the bottom.
common_errors.straight_leg_not_remaining_straight: The non-lunging leg must remain extended throughout for the exercise to properly stretch and eccentrically load the adductors; bending this leg converts the movement toward a side squat and reduces the hip mobility and adductor benefits.
common_errors.torso_rounding_forward: Losing a neutral spine and pitching the chest toward the stepping knee reduces glute activation and increases lumbar stress — the torso should lean only slightly forward in a hip-hinge pattern, not round from the thoracic spine.
common_errors.no_hip_hinge: Squatting straight down rather than hinging back through the hips as the foot steps out overloads the knee extensors and prevents the gluteus medius and posterior hip from doing their stabilizing work; the sensation should be of sitting backward and outward, not just downward.

common_errors.shrugging_traps: Allowing the upper trapezius to elevate the shoulder girdle as the arms are raised — this shifts activation away from the medial deltoid and onto the trapezius, which is already typically overworked, and coaches should cue lifters to keep the shoulder blades anchored down and back throughout the entire movement.
common_errors.using_momentum: Swinging or cheating the dumbbells up with body momentum rather than controlled deltoid abduction — this dramatically reduces medial deltoid time-under-tension, and research confirms that lateral raise is one of the exercises most commonly loaded too heavily; lighter weight with control produces superior deltoid hypertrophy.
common_errors.elbow_position_wrong: Raising with locked-out straight elbows or conversely bent elbows forming an acute angle — the optimal arm position is a slight 5–10° elbow bend throughout; fully locked-out elbows increases wrist torque while a deeply bent elbow reduces the moment arm and therefore the load on the deltoid.
common_errors.raising_above_shoulder_height: Lifting the dumbbells significantly above shoulder height to vertical or beyond — above 90° abduction the supraspinatus tendon enters the impingement zone between the acromion and humeral head, creating a repetitive stress injury risk with high-volume training.
common_errors.internal_rotation_at_bottom: Starting the lift with the thumbs pointing down or the palms fully facing behind rather than toward the thighs — excessive internal rotation narrows the subacromial space, increasing impingement risk and shifting the exercise away from medial deltoid abduction toward a scapular plane movement.

common_errors.excessive_weight: Using a load that causes torso movement, swinging, or grinding through the range of motion — defeats the isolation purpose of the exercise and places excessive compressive and shear forces on the patellar tendon and articular cartilage. This is especially dangerous for athletes with existing knee pathology.
common_errors.incomplete_extension: Not fully extending the leg at the top of each rep — reduces vastus medialis oblique (VMO) activation, which occurs primarily in the final 30 degrees of knee extension and is critical for patellofemoral tracking and knee stability.
common_errors.hard_lockout: Hyperextending and slamming the knee into full lockout — places impact stress on the joint instead of maintaining muscular tension. Extend to full range but under muscular control, not momentum.
common_errors.lifting_hips: Butt rising off the seat during the extension — indicates too much weight and recruits hip flexors to assist, compromising the quad isolation and altering the joint mechanics of the exercise.
common_errors.improper_pad_position: Pad positioned too high on the shin (near the knee) rather than just above the ankle — reduces the leverage available to the quadriceps and increases direct stress on the knee joint. The pad should rest just above the ankle joint.

common_errors.insufficient_depth: Not lowering the platform until the thighs approach the chest — reduces range of motion and gluteus maximus activation significantly. Often ego-driven to allow heavier loads. Depth should bring the knees to roughly 90 degrees or beyond depending on mobility.
common_errors.knee_valgus: Knees caving inward during the press — same hip abductor weakness pattern as in free-weight squats. The knee tracking should stay aligned with the second toe throughout the entire range of motion.
common_errors.lower_back_rounding: Pelvis tilting posteriorly at the bottom of the movement — occurs when the athlete goes beyond their hip mobility, causing the lumbar spine to flex under load and risking disc injury. The lower back must remain in contact with the pad.
common_errors.locking_knees: Hyperextending the knees to full lockout at the top of each rep — transfers all compressive force directly onto the knee joint instead of maintaining muscular tension. Stop just short of full extension to keep tension in the quadriceps.
common_errors.feet_too_low: Placing the feet very low on the platform to maximize quad isolation — while it does increase quadriceps demand, it also dramatically increases shear force on the patellar tendon and is inappropriate for athletes with any history of knee issues.

common_errors.insufficient_warm_up_and_progressive_exp: Attempting maximum-effort sprints without a thorough progressive warm-up — or returning to sprint training after extended inactivity without gradually rebuilding tissue tolerance over weeks — is the primary driver of hamstring strains, calf tears, and Achilles injuries in sprint training. Athletes must perform dynamic warm-up, build through progressive run-throughs at 50%, 70%, and 85% effort, and resist the urge to immediately test top speed.
common_errors.inadequate_rest_between_efforts: Treating sprint work as conditioning by taking short 30–60 second rests between efforts means the athlete is never recovering enough to express true maximal speed — they are running at 70–80% effort and calling it sprinting. True speed development requires 1:12 to 1:20 work-to-rest ratios: a 5-second sprint demands 1–2 minutes of full rest before the next rep can be performed at genuine maximum intensity.
common_errors.overstriding: Reaching the lead foot too far in front of the body's center of mass creates a braking force on every ground contact that decelerates the athlete and increases hamstring strain risk as the posterior chain works to pull the body over the extended foot. Sprint mechanics emphasize driving the foot down and back under the hip, not reaching forward — the cue is 'paw the ground' rather than 'reach for the ground.'
common_errors.insufficient_strength_foundation: Athletes without adequate lower body strength — particularly in single-leg hip extension, hamstring control, and calf resilience — who begin high-intensity sprint training are at significantly elevated injury risk because the forces generated during max-effort sprinting (up to 3–5x bodyweight) exceed the tissue capacity of underprepared muscles and tendons. Foundational strength in bilateral and unilateral lower body movements should precede intensive sprint development.
common_errors.training_only_one_speed: Athletes who exclusively train aerobic conditioning or moderate-intensity running develop metabolic fitness without ever recruiting the fast-twitch motor units that produce top-end speed — and fast-twitch fibers left undertrained atrophy preferentially. True sprint development requires dedicated sessions of near-maximal and maximal efforts with full recovery, completely separate from conditioning work, to develop and preserve fast-twitch capacity.

common_errors.arm_dominant_clean: Muscling the log from the lap to the chest using arm strength rather than hip pop and leg drive — the clean phase must initiate with explosive hip extension so that the log travels up the torso under momentum, not bicep contraction. Arm-dominant cleaning pre-fatigues the pressing muscles and dramatically limits the weight that can be pressed.
common_errors.log_too_low_on_chest: Racking the log in the mid-chest rather than up high on the upper chest/collarbone area — a low rack increases the effective moment arm and puts the athlete in a mechanically weak position for the press initiation. The log's large diameter means a high rack is essential for the push press to be efficient.
common_errors.elbow_position_collapse: Allowing elbows to drop before the press drive rather than keeping them high and wide — elbows should stay elevated so the athlete can use the chest and upper back to help initiate the drive, not just the deltoids. Low elbows are a direct predictor of missed attempts on heavy logs.
common_errors.insufficient_leg_drive_in_push_press: Pressing with arms only rather than using a dip-and-drive push press technique, particularly evident in athletes with good strict press strength who try to power through without learning the leg contribution. A proper dip of 4-6 inches followed by an explosive hip extension can add 20-40% to the amount of log a trained athlete can press.
common_errors.not_controlling_descent: In competition repetition-style events, dropping or 'crashing' the log back to the chest rather than controlling the descent loads the shoulder joint eccentrically under an uncontrolled rate and is a primary injury mechanism — particularly for the rotator cuff and AC joint.

common_errors.hip_lifting: Hips rising off the pad during the curl — indicates the weight is too heavy and the athlete is using hip flexion to assist the movement. Reduces hamstring isolation entirely and can strain the lower back. The hips must stay flat on the pad throughout.
common_errors.using_momentum: Swinging the weight up and dropping it down — eliminates the muscular tension that drives hypertrophy. Every rep should be controlled, especially the eccentric lowering phase where hamstring growth stimulus is highest.
common_errors.incomplete_range: Not curling the heels all the way toward the glutes — reduces the peak contraction at the shortened position of the hamstrings. Full range means heels travel as close to the glutes as the machine allows.
common_errors.neck_strain: Lifting the head off the pad to watch the weight move — creates unnecessary cervical spine compression throughout the set. Head should remain in a neutral position resting on the pad or hands.
common_errors.foot_rotation: Allowing the feet to rotate outward or inward during the curl — external rotation increases biceps femoris contribution; internal rotation shifts load to semitendinosus and semimembranosus. For balanced development, keep feet neutral and toes pointing straight down.

common_errors.arms_dominating_the_throw: Pushing the ball primarily with the arms rather than generating power from the ground up through the hips and trunk rotation — the kinetic chain for rotational power starts with the back foot push, the hip opening, and the torso driving; the arms should transmit and accelerate that force, not produce it.
common_errors.incomplete_hip_rotation: Failing to fully rotate the hips in the direction of the throw — athletes who block off their hips and throw with the upper body only are generating force from the lumbar spine rather than true rotational power. The back foot should pivot, the back knee should drive inward, and the pelvis should lead the shoulders.
common_errors.no_countermovement_load: Not rotating into a preloaded backswing before throwing — the rotational throw is a stretch-shortening cycle movement and requires a countermovement rotation to pre-stretch the obliques and build elastic contribution to throw velocity.
common_errors.ball_too_heavy: Using a load that forces a grinding, slow rotation rather than an explosive hip-to-shoulder transfer — rotational throws are speed-strength movements and the ball should be light enough to maintain maximal intent throughout. Heavy ball work has its place, but high-velocity rotational power requires appropriate loading.
common_errors.front_foot_collapsing: Allowing the front foot to toe out excessively or the front knee to cave inward as the throw completes — the front leg acts as a blocking post to decelerate the lower body and accelerate the upper body through; a collapsing front leg bleeds force laterally and places valgus stress on the knee.

common_errors.no_triple_extension_at_top: Not achieving full hip, knee, and ankle extension at the overhead position before initiating the slam — the power of the downward phase is proportional to the height and tension achieved at the top. Rounding the back and shortening the reach underloads the lats and core in the eccentric stretch phase.
common_errors.arm_dominated_slam: Pulling the ball down primarily with the arms rather than driving the slam by bracing and explosively flexing the trunk — the core should initiate the downward force, with the lats and arms accelerating the ball. Pure arm-pulling reduces force output and loses the abdominal training stimulus.
common_errors.passive_ball_retrieval: Casually picking up the ball rather than immediately squatting down to collect it and returning to start explosively — in power training contexts, inefficient transitions between reps diffuse the training focus and reduce total power output per unit time.
common_errors.ball_too_heavy: Using a ball so heavy it distorts the overhead position or forces a grinding, controlled movement rather than a ballistic slam — the ball should be light enough to accelerate explosively through the full range. A ball weight that compromises the full overhead extension defeats the purpose.
common_errors.no_core_bracing: Failing to brace the trunk through the slam, allowing the lumbar spine to hyperextend at the overhead position or hyperflex at impact — a firm neutral spine throughout protects the discs and ensures force transfers from the whole-body movement into the ball.

common_errors.band_at_knees_only: Using a single band around the knees rather than at the ankles (or using two bands — one at knees, one at ankles — for true monster walk variation) dramatically reduces the resistance lever arm and diminishes glute medius activation; ankle placement provides a greater moment arm and higher EMG output.
common_errors.skipping_squat_position: Walking upright instead of maintaining a partial squat throughout the set removes the hip-flexed context that maximally loads the abductors and shifts recruitment toward the TFL — staying in a quarter-squat throughout is essential to the exercise's purpose.
common_errors.too_large_steps: Overstriding causes the pelvis to drop on the swinging side (Trendelenburg sign) as the abductors are overpowered by the step, reducing targeted activation and reinforcing poor movement patterns rather than correcting them.
common_errors.only_lateral_direction: Restricting the exercise to purely lateral movement omits the diagonal and forward/backward directions that make the monster walk distinct from the lateral band walk — full programming should include all vectors to train the gluteals tri-planarly.
common_errors.rushing_pace: Moving too quickly turns this into a cardiovascular shuffle rather than a controlled neuromuscular activation drill; slow, deliberate steps (1–2 seconds per step) allow the gluteus medius to maintain full isometric and concentric demand rather than relying on momentum.

common_errors.hip_flexion: Bending at the hip as the body lowers — the hips must stay fully extended throughout the entire descent so the hamstrings are the only joint doing work. This is the single most common error and completely eliminates the exercise's training stimulus.
common_errors.collapsing_too_fast: Dropping to the floor immediately rather than resisting the descent — the entire training value is in the slow, controlled eccentric. Athletes who cannot control at least 2 seconds of lowering should regress to a band-assisted version.
common_errors.rushing_concentric: Pushing aggressively off the floor to return to start — the push-off should be minimal and serve only to reset position, not to power the movement.
common_errors.unsecured_ankles: Feet not anchored firmly enough, causing the anchor to shift mid-rep and transferring load away from the hamstrings.
common_errors.asymmetry: One side lowering faster or further than the other — often reveals a bilateral hamstring strength imbalance that is worth flagging and addressing directly.

common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: Excessively arching the lower back to compensate for limited shoulder or thoracic mobility — this compresses the lumbar spine under axial load and is a primary driver of lower back injury in overhead pressing; it almost always indicates insufficient thoracic extension or hip flexor tightness that should be addressed in warmup.
common_errors.bar_path_forward: Pressing the bar in a straight vertical line in front of the face rather than allowing the head to move through the 'window' so the bar finishes directly over the midfoot — a bar that stays forward of the body's center of mass creates a large moment arm at the shoulder and dramatically reduces mechanical efficiency and safe loading capacity.
common_errors.no_leg_drive_or_core_bracing: Failing to create a rigid torso through a Valsalva breath and full-body tension before pressing — the standing overhead press is a full-body lift and any energy leak between the floor and the bar (loose core, soft knees) reduces maximal force transmission and increases spinal injury risk.
common_errors.elbow_position_too_forward: Starting with the elbows pointed directly forward so the bar rests far down on the deltoids rather than in the heel of the hand over the forearm — elbows should be slightly in front of the bar at setup (not behind, not excessively forward) to optimize wrist and shoulder alignment for the press.
common_errors.collapsing_wrists: Allowing the wrists to bend backward under the bar instead of keeping them stacked neutral over the elbows — this creates pain at the wrist joint and reduces structural integrity of the pressing chain, effectively wasting force that should go into moving the bar.

common_errors.elbows_flaring_outward: The most universal form error — allowing the elbows to spread wide removes the stretch from the long head and substitutes shoulder abduction for elbow extension. Elbows should stay pointed directly upward and narrow, tracking no wider than shoulder-width throughout the movement.
common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: The overhead position creates a strong anterior pull that most lifters compensate for by arching the lower back excessively. This increases lumbar disc compression and defeats the shoulder flexion needed to fully stretch the long head. A braced core and rib-cage down cue prevents this.
common_errors.insufficient_range_of_motion: Not lowering the weight deep enough behind the head to reach a fully stretched long-head position is the most common cause of the exercise underperforming relative to its potential. Research on training at long muscle lengths shows significantly greater hypertrophy when full depth is achieved.
common_errors.upper_arms_drifting_forward: As fatigue accumulates, the upper arms tend to migrate from vertical toward a forward angle, which progressively shifts the movement toward a pushing pattern and away from the pure elbow-extension isolation of the long head. Upper arms must stay perpendicular to the floor or slightly angled back.
common_errors.excessive_load_without_shoulder_mobility: Attempting too heavy a load before adequate shoulder and thoracic mobility leads to compensatory lumbar arch, cervical strain, and reduced range of motion — all of which reduce the exercise's effectiveness and increase injury risk. Coaches recommend progressing load only after full overhead ROM is achieved without compensation.

common_errors.rotating_the_torso: Allowing the torso to twist toward the cable or band during the press and return — a fundamental failure to meet the exercise's singular demand. The entire training stimulus is anti-rotation; any trunk rotation means the obliques have not produced sufficient isometric tension to fulfill their role.
common_errors.leaning_into_the_pull: Side-bending toward the cable as a compensation strategy rather than maintaining a vertical torso. This is a subtler error than full rotation but it similarly redirects load away from the anti-rotation stabilizers and into the lateral flexors, which is not the intended stimulus.
common_errors.too_much_weight: Selecting a load that cannot be resisted isometrically without compensatory body movement. Unlike most loaded exercises, heavier is not better here — the Pallof press is most effective at the lightest load that creates meaningful anti-rotation challenge while allowing perfect posture.
common_errors.feet_too_close: Standing with a narrow stance that reduces the stable base needed to resist the lateral pull. Shoulder-width feet with soft knees create the foundation; without adequate base of support, the lower body compensates with lateral sway rather than the core providing anti-rotation resistance.
common_errors.rushing_the_press: Pressing quickly in and out without pausing in the extended position, which eliminates the peak anti-rotation demand. The outstretched arms create the longest possible moment arm; pausing there forces the obliques to work at maximum disadvantage, which is precisely where the training effect is greatest.

common_errors.using_ridged_plates: Choosing knurled or rubber-edged plates rather than smooth-sided iron plates. Textured plates provide enough friction that the fingers can hold on passively, eliminating the pinch-specific thenar demand that is the entire point of the exercise. Smooth iron plates are standard in grip sport for this reason.
common_errors.improper_thumb_position: Placing the thumb on the same face of the plate as the fingers rather than wrapping it around the opposite side. True pinch grip requires the thumb to oppose the fingers with the plate squeezed between them; a lateral thumb merely converts the movement to a hook grip and de-loads the thenar musculature.
common_errors.too_short_hold_times: Releasing after 5–10 seconds as if this were a dynamic exercise. Pinch strength is a sustained isometric quality; 20–45 second holds per set are standard in grip sport programming, and the primary adaptation is both maximal thumb flexion force and thenar muscular endurance.
common_errors.overloading_too_fast: Progressing plate weight before the thumb can fully oppose the load. Rapid overload shifts force onto the flexor pollicis longus tendon and its insertion at the distal phalanx, a common site of tendinopathy in grip athletes. Weight should increase only when the current load can be held for the full target duration with no hand position breakdown.

common_errors.hip_sagging: Allowing the hips and lower back to drop toward the floor — the most universally observed plank error. This eliminates anti-extension demand on the abdominals and compresses the lumbar spine, converting the exercise from a core stability drill into a passive lumbar hyperextension hold.
common_errors.hip_piking: Raising the hips too high so the body forms an inverted V rather than a straight line. This offloads the core and transfers the work to the shoulders and hamstrings, completely undermining the spinal bracing stimulus the plank is intended to produce.
common_errors.excessive_duration: Holding planks for minutes at a time while form progressively deteriorates — a product of the pop-culture plank challenge mentality. Elite coaches including Stuart McGill recommend short, high-quality 10-second holds with multiple sets; endurance past the point of postural breakdown produces spinal loading with no additional training benefit.
common_errors.forward_head_position: Letting the neck drop so the chin juts forward or the head hangs between the arms. This disrupts the neutral cervical alignment that should be maintained as part of the straight-line position from ears to heels.
common_errors.scapular_winging: Allowing the shoulder blades to collapse inward rather than actively protracting and depressing them. This reduces proximal stability, shifts load into the passive shoulder structures, and is especially common in high-plank (straight-arm) variations.

common_errors.early_arm_bend: Flexing the elbows before triple extension is complete — 'when the arms bend, the power ends.' This shifts force generation from the large hip and leg extensors to the small biceps, dramatically reducing bar height and robbing the lift of its explosive training stimulus.
common_errors.hips_rising_faster_than_shoulders: Letting the hips shoot up faster than the shoulders during the first pull converts the movement into a stiff-leg deadlift and places the lifter in a mechanically disadvantaged position before the second pull; shoulders and hips must rise at the same rate until the bar clears the knees.
common_errors.bar_drifting_away: Allowing the bar to swing out from the body during the pull increases the moment arm and makes the catch position nearly impossible at heavy loads; the bar should trace a tight S-curve path staying within an inch of the shins and thighs throughout.
common_errors.no_full_triple_extension: Cutting the second pull short by jumping forward instead of vertically — full simultaneous extension of the ankles, knees, and hips is required to impart maximum upward velocity to the bar before dropping under it.
common_errors.wide_catch_stance: Landing with the feet excessively wide to receive the bar indicates the lifter is jumping out rather than pulling under; an excessively wide receiving stance destabilizes the front rack and cannot be fed directly into a front squat.
common_errors.soft_starting_position: Beginning with slack in the arms or a rounded upper back at setup; any slack in the system means the first force applied by the legs is wasted tightening slack rather than moving the bar, resulting in a jerky liftoff and compromised first pull mechanics.

common_errors.incomplete_extension: Rushing under the bar before achieving full triple extension — hips, knees, and ankles must all reach full lock before the lifter drops; cutting extension early prevents the bar from reaching adequate height and results in a forward-leaning catch that cannot be safely controlled overhead.
common_errors.bar_swinging_forward: Excessive forward bar path caused by bumping the hips too hard horizontally rather than vertically during the second pull; a violent horizontal hip drive sends the bar in an arc away from the body, making the catch position dangerously unstable.
common_errors.pressing_out_overhead: Finishing the lift by muscling the bar to lockout with the arms rather than catching it with elbows fully extended; this indicates the second pull was too short and is a no-lift in competition — athletes should focus on achieving maximum bar speed before committing to the pull-under.
common_errors.hips_rising_faster_than_shoulders: The same first-pull error seen in the power clean: hips shooting up faster than shoulders converts the setup into a stiff-leg pull, eliminating quadriceps contribution from the drive phase and setting up a compromised second pull.
common_errors.soft_overhead_position: Receiving the bar with soft elbows or a forward lean in the catch; overhead stability in the power snatch demands aggressive lock-out with the bar behind the ears and the scapulae actively retracted — failure to create this stable shelf immediately loads the wrist and shoulder joints.

common_errors.hyperextending_at_the_bottom: Allowing the elbows to fully lock out aggressively at the bottom of the rep places extreme tensile stress on the distal biceps tendon at its most vulnerable length. The arm should be lowered under control to near-full extension without snapping into the lockout.
common_errors.pad_positioned_too_high: When the top of the pad sits above the lower pectoral line, only the lower biceps and brachialis engage and the upper/peak portion of the biceps is excluded. Correct pad height allows the elbow to just clear the top so the full biceps can be loaded through the complete ROM — as originally specified by Vince Gironda.
common_errors.shortening_the_eccentric: Dropping the weight quickly on the descent after a controlled concentric eliminates the stretched-position loading that is the anatomical advantage of the preacher curl. Research shows the biceps produces the most hypertrophic stimulus in the lengthened position, making a slow eccentric critical here.
common_errors.excessive_weight_causing_momentum: Ego loading on the preacher curl results in the torso leaning into the pad and the shoulder driving forward — both of which introduce deltoid assistance and defeat the purpose of the exercise. The pad is meant to lock out momentum, so the weight should be lighter than a standing curl.
common_errors.wrist_flexion_under_load: Breaking the wrist into flexion at the top transfers the contraction stress from the biceps to the forearm flexors and can create medial wrist pain over time. The wrist must stay neutral through the full range of motion.

common_errors.anterior_tilt_and_protraction: Allowing the shoulder blades to roll forward and protract as the arms lift reduces middle trapezius and rhomboid activation because those muscles are the agonists of retraction — the primary cue is to actively retract and depress the scapulae before and during the lift.
common_errors.arms_not_at_90_degrees: Raising the arms at an angle other than 90° to the torso (i.e., not forming a true T shape) shifts the load from the middle trapezius toward either the lower or upper trapezius. Precise 90° abduction is required to isolate the middle trapezius fibers.
common_errors.upper_trap_shrugging: Elevating the shoulders as the arms rise recruits the upper trapezius and reduces the specificity of the exercise for the middle trapezius and rhomboids. Cue shoulder blade depression throughout the entire range of motion.
common_errors.excessive_weight: Loading too heavily causes the torso to rotate or the spine to hyperextend to generate momentum, turning a controlled scapular drill into a compensatory back extension movement. This exercise works best with very light weight and slow tempo.
common_errors.no_end_range_hold: Not pausing with maximum retraction at end range eliminates the isometric peak contraction that drives neuromuscular re-education of the middle trapezius — a 1–2 second hold at the top of each repetition is a critical coaching cue for any patient with scapular dyskinesis.

common_errors.insufficient_external_rotation: Failing to rotate the forearms upward into the goalpost (W) position and simply raising the elbows instead removes the rotator cuff component entirely — the whole purpose of the W over the T is the combined horizontal abduction plus external rotation, and the forearm angle must reach vertical.
common_errors.scapular_elevation: Shrugging the shoulders upward to achieve arm height substitutes upper trapezius for the intended middle trapezius and infraspinatus activation — the scapulae must remain depressed throughout, with motion coming from glenohumeral rotation, not scapular elevation.
common_errors.restricted_thoracic_spine: Attempting this exercise without adequate thoracic extension mobility forces compensatory lumbar extension and forward head position. In patients with significant thoracic kyphosis the exercise should first be performed on an incline bench to allow the thoracic spine to extend passively.
common_errors.momentum_use: Using a ballistic lift defeats the slow eccentric-concentric tempo that builds the neuromuscular control and endurance the exercise is prescribed to develop — the W raise is a quality-over-quantity exercise where 10 controlled reps outperforms 30 sloppy ones.
common_errors.elbows_too_far_forward: Positioning the elbows forward of the shoulder plane rather than directly out to the side at 90° abduction changes the shoulder mechanics, increases impingement risk in sensitized shoulders, and reduces posterior rotator cuff activation.

common_errors.upper_trap_substitution: Shrugging the shoulders upward as the arms lift is the most common error and reflects lower trapezius weakness — the scapulae must depress and posteriorly tilt as the arms rise, not elevate. This error directly defeats the lower trapezius training stimulus that is the entire purpose of the exercise.
common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: Arching the lower back to achieve greater arm lift height compensates for limited shoulder flexion and upper thoracic mobility, removing tension from the lower trapezius and loading the lumbar spine. The lift should originate from the shoulder blade, not spinal extension.
common_errors.excessive_load: Using too much dumbbell weight causes the movement to be dominated by trunk extension and scapular compensation rather than true shoulder elevation in the Y plane — the Ekstrom EMG data shows the exercise is most effective at high relative intensity with arms in the lower trap fiber direction, which most people can barely achieve with a light weight.
common_errors.wrong_arm_angle: Raising the arms in a true overhead position (180° shoulder flexion, straight up) rather than angled at approximately 135° — aligned with the lower trapezius muscle fibers — drastically reduces lower trapezius specificity. The Y shape is critical: arms angled outward at roughly 45° from the midline.
common_errors.no_thumb_up_cue: Performing the raise with palms facing down (pronated) instead of thumbs up (externally rotated) closes the subacromial space and reduces lower trapezius activation. The thumbs-up position cues the shoulder into external rotation, which is required for optimal scapular mechanics and subacromial clearance.

common_errors.load_too_heavy_for_intended_stimulus: Loading the sled so heavily that movement speed drops to a slow grinding march when the goal is speed or power development — heavy loads shift the training adaptation entirely toward maximal strength and eliminate the sprint mechanics and fast-twitch recruitment the session was designed for. Loads for speed work should allow near-sprint velocity; if the athlete cannot accelerate aggressively out of the start, the load is too heavy for that purpose.
common_errors.torso_too_upright: Pushing with the torso close to vertical rather than leaning aggressively forward at roughly 45 degrees or more — an upright position means the force vector is directed downward into the ground rather than horizontally into the sled, dramatically increasing the effective friction load and reducing forward propulsion. The athlete should lean so far forward that the shoulders are nearly level with or below the handles, creating a straight line of force from the rear foot through the torso to the sled.
common_errors.bent_arm_pushing: Allowing the elbows to bend during the push rather than maintaining locked, extended arms — bent arms absorb force in the shoulder and elbow joints rather than transferring it rigidly through the torso and into the sled. The arms should function as rigid struts, with force generated entirely by the legs and transmitted through a braced core and locked arms into the handles.
common_errors.short_choppy_strides: Taking rapid small steps rather than long powerful strides reduces ground contact force per step and limits acceleration. Each stride should drive aggressively into the surface with the full foot, extending forcefully through the hip and knee, similar to a sprint start acceleration mechanic.
common_errors.neglecting_surface_variation: Failing to adjust load based on the training surface — a prowler that moves easily on smooth rubber flooring may feel twice as heavy on dry concrete and several times heavier on wet grass. Coaches should calibrate loads per surface and athletes should not assume a prescribed weight translates across environments.

common_errors.scapular_elevation_at_initiation: Beginning the pull by shrugging the shoulders toward the ears rather than first depressing and retracting the scapulae — this shifts primary load to the upper trapezius and cervical spine instead of the latissimus dorsi, dramatically reducing the training stimulus for the intended musculature.
common_errors.forward_head_protrusion: Craning the neck forward to clear the bar rather than maintaining a neutral cervical spine — a compensation pattern for insufficient lat strength that increases shear stress on the cervical vertebrae and indicates the load exceeds the athlete's current capacity.
common_errors.incomplete_range_of_motion: Not achieving full elbow extension at the bottom or failing to bring the chin definitively above the bar at the top — partial reps allow the athlete to avoid the most mechanically demanding portions of the lift and accumulate less actual lat training volume.
common_errors.excessive_momentum_and_swinging: Using hip drive, knee kick, or body oscillation to assist each rep in a context where strict form is intended — while kipping is a legitimate variation, unintentional swinging in a strict set reduces time under tension, masks strength deficits, and increases shoulder instability risk.
common_errors.elbows_not_tracking_toward_lats: Allowing elbows to flare excessively wide rather than driving them down and back toward the hip — correct elbow path is what mechanically recruits the lats through their primary function of shoulder adduction and extension.

common_errors.pressing_out_to_finish: Cutting the drive short so the bar doesn't reach full lockout height, then muscling it overhead with the arms — the most common jerk fault at beginner to intermediate level and a no-lift in competition; the drive must be aggressive enough that the bar reaches lockout height passively as the lifter drops under it.
common_errors.forward_lean_during_dip: Allowing the torso to tilt forward during the dip causes the bar to be launched forward off the shoulders rather than vertically, making the catch position unstable and forward; the dip must keep the torso absolutely vertical.
common_errors.slow_or_hesitant_rebend: Pausing at the top of the drive before actively dropping under the bar causes the lifter to miss the window when the bar is momentarily weightless; the transition from drive to drop must be immediate and aggressive with no pause.
common_errors.feet_not_actively_landing: Some athletes freeze their feet in the drive position rather than actively re-stabilizing under the bar; even in a push jerk where footwork is minimal, the feet must land flat and simultaneously with the lockout to create a stable base.
common_errors.soft_catch_position: Receiving the bar with unlocked elbows or a forward-traveling torso rather than a rigid overhead squat position — the receiving position in a push jerk is a partial overhead squat and demands the same braced midline and active shoulder lock as any overhead squat.

common_errors.excessive_lumbar_extension_during_dip: Arching the lower back rather than maintaining a vertical torso through the dip-and-drive; this loses the rigid midline needed to transfer leg force to the bar and can place dangerous shear on lumbar discs under load — core must remain braced and trunk vertical throughout the dip.
common_errors.pressing_before_full_hip_extension: Beginning the overhead press before the legs have fully driven the hips to extension squanders the leg-drive contribution, forcing the triceps and deltoids to press weight the legs should have already accelerated — the cue is to 'drive legs, then press,' not to blend them simultaneously.
common_errors.elbows_dropping_in_rack_position: Allowing the elbows to fall below the bar during the setup and dip compromises the front rack shelf, causing the bar to roll forward onto the wrists and making force transfer from torso to bar inefficient and painful under heavy load.
common_errors.forward_bar_path: Pressing the bar slightly forward rather than straight up results in a longer moment arm at the shoulder and often causes the lifter to lean back to compensate, increasing risk of lumbar strain; the bar must travel vertically over the midfoot.
common_errors.shallow_dip: A dip of only a few millimetres provides insufficient impulse to assist the press; elite coaches cue a deliberate 2-4 inch dip with the knees tracking over the toes and the torso remaining completely upright before the aggressive drive.

common_errors.sagging_hips: Allowing the lumbar spine and hips to drop toward the floor rather than maintaining a rigid plank position — this compresses the lumbar spine under load, deactivates the core stabilizers that give the push-up its functional value, and converts the exercise into a partial movement that underloads the intended muscles.
common_errors.piking_hips: Raising the hips into the air during the movement, often as a compensation for insufficient pressing strength — this reduces the load through the upper body by transferring it to the lower body, and the lifter is no longer performing a full push-up.
common_errors.elbows_flaring_perpendicular: Allowing the elbows to splay out at 90° to the torso (T-position) rather than tracking at 45–75° — this is the single most common push-up error and the primary contributor to shoulder impingement during high-volume push-up training in military and athletic populations.
common_errors.incomplete_range_of_motion: Not descending until the chest nearly touches the floor, or not pressing to full elbow extension — partial reps reduce pectoralis and serratus anterior activation and train a false strength through an incomplete range, limiting both hypertrophic and strength adaptations.
common_errors.forward_head_position: Allowing the head to jut forward during the descent so the chin reaches the floor first — this hyperextends the cervical spine under compression and teaches poor spinal alignment habits that transfer to pressing movements; the neck should remain neutral, part of the rigid plank.

common_errors.using_supinated_curl_weight: Athletes habitually attempt reverse curls with the same load they use for standard biceps curls. Because the biceps is mechanically disadvantaged in pronation and its supinator function is deactivated, the brachioradialis and brachialis must do more work with less assistance — necessitating a 30–50% load reduction.
common_errors.wrist_flexion_collapse: The pronated position demands active wrist extension throughout the curl, but when the load is too heavy the wrists collapse into flexion, stressing the extensor carpi tendons and reducing loading on the primary target muscles. Neutral-to-slightly-extended wrists must be actively maintained.
common_errors.elbow_drift_forward: As in all curl variations, the elbows drifting forward at the top recruits the anterior deltoid to assist and takes load off the brachioradialis. This is particularly problematic in the reverse curl because the anterior deltoid activates more in the pronated grip condition, making strict elbow position even more critical.
common_errors.swinging_and_momentum: Because the brachioradialis is a relatively small muscle compared to the biceps, even small amounts of body swing dramatically unload it. The exercise should be performed in strict fashion with a controlled tempo, prioritizing muscle tension over weight moved.
common_errors.neglecting_full_extension: Reverse curls performed through a partial range of motion at the bottom deprive the brachioradialis and brachialis of their stretched-position stimulus. A full return to elbow extension on each rep is necessary to capitalize on the length-tension relationship of these muscles.

common_errors.blocking_spinal_traction: Being too rigid through the lumbar spine on the descent and not allowing the sacrum to naturally tilt — the reverse hyper's key therapeutic benefit is spinal decompression on the lowering phase. Gripping or bracing hard against this motion eliminates the traction effect that makes the exercise valuable for back health.
common_errors.not_bracing_abs_into_pad: Failing to press the abdomen firmly into the pad throughout the movement — without this anterior pressure, the lumbar spine is unsupported and can hyperextend rather than staying in neutral during hip extension. Cue: 'push your belly button through the pad.'
common_errors.lifting_legs_too_high: Swinging the legs above horizontal, which causes lumbar hyperextension rather than pure hip extension — the legs should rise to approximately parallel with the floor at the top, no higher. Excessive range comes from the lower back, not the hips.
common_errors.using_momentum_not_hip_drive: Kipping or using body sway to generate swing rather than deliberate hip extension — this converts the exercise into a ballistic lower back movement and removes the controlled eccentric that provides the traction benefit.
common_errors.asymmetrical_leg_movement: One leg driving higher than the other or the legs splitting apart during the movement, indicating unilateral hip extensor weakness or hip mobility asymmetry. The legs should move as a single unit through the full range.

common_errors.front_knee_caving: The front knee collapsing medially during the descent is a combination of hip abductor weakness and failure to actively externally rotate the hip on the way down. It places shear force on the medial knee structures and, in high-volume training, is a reliable path to patellofemoral pain — the knee must track directly over the second toe throughout.
common_errors.inconsistent_step_length: Taking a step that is either too long or too short each rep destabilizes the movement pattern, makes tracking progress impossible, and produces inconsistent muscle loading. Too short a step compresses the front knee past the toes and biases quads at the expense of glutes; too long a step increases hip flexion demand beyond what can be controlled and often causes lumbar compensation.
common_errors.back_knee_not_reaching_floor: Stopping the descent high above the floor — often out of discomfort or fear — significantly reduces hip flexor length and glute stretch on the back leg side, and limits quad range of motion on the front leg. The back knee should lower to within 1-2 inches of the floor on every rep.
common_errors.torso_leaning_excessively_forward: Pitching the trunk forward over the front leg shifts load onto the hip extensors and reduces quad involvement — this may be intentional as a glute-focused variation but is rarely coached that way. For a quad-balanced reverse lunge the chest stays upright, shoulder blades back, and the front shin remains mostly vertical.
common_errors.using_momentum_to_return: Pushing explosively off the back foot to return to standing rather than using a deliberate front-leg drive reduces the time the quad and glute are under load and increases the injury risk during the push-off. The front heel drives the return; the rear foot is simply lifted away, not pushed from.

common_errors.excessive_forward_lean: Leaning too far forward from the hips during the backward walk, which shifts the load from the quadriceps onto the back and glutes and compresses the lumbar spine. The torso should remain upright or only very slightly forward-inclined so that each step mimics a terminal knee extension pattern.
common_errors.overstriding: Taking excessively long backward steps, which prevents the knee from going through its full extension range on each stride and reduces the per-step loading of the quadriceps. Short, controlled steps that allow full knee extension with each backward stride maximize the therapeutic effect.
common_errors.loading_too_heavy_too_soon: Starting with heavy sled loads before establishing proper mechanics, causing technique breakdown and potentially aggravating the very knee condition the exercise is designed to treat. Reverse sled drags should be initiated with light to moderate loads — Ben Patrick recommends starting at roughly half bodyweight — and progressed conservatively.
common_errors.attaching_to_wrists_or_arms: Using arm handles or wrist loops rather than a hip belt or harness, which turns the exercise into an upper-body drag and reduces the quad stimulus. The resistance should be transmitted through the hips so the legs drive each stride.
common_errors.using_a_wheeled_sled: Using a sled with wheels rather than a friction sled, which allows the sled to follow the athlete without providing consistent resistance and diminishes the constant quad tension that makes this exercise therapeutically effective for knee rehab and patellar tendon loading.

common_errors.too_heavy_a_load: Using similar weight to the wrist curl because the movement looks similar. The wrist extensors are significantly weaker than the flexors (roughly 50–60% as strong); most individuals should use 40–60% of their wrist curl load. Overloading is the primary cause of irritating the common extensor tendon origin at the lateral epicondyle.
common_errors.forearm_not_supported: Performing the movement with the forearm unsupported or hanging loosely, which allows elbow extension and shoulder mechanics to compensate and masks wrist extensor weakness. The forearm must lie flat with the wrist hanging just off the edge of a bench or knee.
common_errors.rushing_the_eccentric: Dropping the wrist rapidly back to the starting position rather than controlling the descent. Eccentric wrist extensor loading is a primary therapeutic mechanism in lateral epicondylitis rehabilitation; a slow, 2–3 second lowering phase maximizes both rehabilitation and hypertrophic stimulus.
common_errors.neglecting_the_exercise_entirely: Never programming reverse wrist curls alongside wrist curls. Bilateral flexor-to-extensor strength imbalance is a well-documented predisposing factor for both medial and lateral epicondylitis; the exercise is rarely performed in proportion to its importance for forearm health.

common_errors.excessive_knee_bend: Bending the knees too much throughout the movement, effectively turning the RDL into a conventional deadlift — defeats the primary purpose of the exercise, which is to isolate the hamstrings through a hip hinge with minimal knee travel. Knees should have a soft, fixed bend.
common_errors.rounding_back: Allowing thoracic or lumbar rounding during the descent — occurs when the athlete goes deeper than their hamstring flexibility allows, shifting tension from the hamstrings to the spinal ligaments and placing the lumbar discs at risk under load.
common_errors.bar_drifting_away: Letting the bar drift forward away from the body — happens when the lats aren't engaged to keep the bar close, dramatically increasing the moment arm at the lower back and reducing hamstring tension. The bar should nearly brush the thighs throughout.
common_errors.rushing_eccentric: Dropping the weight quickly instead of controlling the descent — eliminates the primary hypertrophy stimulus of the RDL, which is the slow, controlled eccentric stretch of the hamstrings under load.
common_errors.going_too_deep: Lowering beyond the natural stopping point dictated by hamstring flexibility — an ego-driven error that forces lumbar rounding to achieve greater depth, shifting the load away from the target muscles and onto the spine.

common_errors.knee_flexion_not_hip_hinge: Bending the knees significantly during the lowering phase converts the movement into a partial deadlift, reducing the hamstring stretch stimulus; the knee angle should remain nearly constant throughout the descent with the hinge driven entirely by hip flexion.
