common_errors.rounding_the_upper_back: Allowing the thoracic and lumbar spine to flex during the descent shifts load from the hamstrings to the spinal erectors and, under heavy loading, increases the risk of disc injury; a neutral spine from tailbone to crown must be maintained throughout.
common_errors.shrug_performed_as_isolation: Performing a deliberate, slow, isolated shoulder shrug after pausing at standing neutralizes the intent of the exercise; the shrug should occur as a natural continuation of hip extension momentum, flowing seamlessly from the upward drive — this pattern transfers to the Olympic lifts the movement is designed to reinforce.
common_errors.bar_drifting_from_legs: Letting the bar drift away from the body during the descent increases the lumbar moment arm dramatically; the bar should stay in contact with or within an inch of the thighs and shins throughout, exactly as it would in the first pull of a clean.
common_errors.hyperextension_at_lockout: Leaning back aggressively at the top of the movement to facilitate the shrug creates excessive lumbar extension under load; the hips should reach full extension with the torso vertical, and the shrug should be initiated with the spine neutral and the glutes engaged.

common_errors.early_arm_bend: Bending the elbows and initiating the arm pull before the legs are fully driven down — this is the single most common error and it short-circuits the kinetic chain by engaging the smallest, weakest muscles before the largest muscles have finished their work. The arms should remain straight like hooks until the legs reach near full extension, at which point the body swings back and only then do the elbows draw back. The cue is 'push not pull' — hang off the handle with straight arms and focus on the leg drive.
common_errors.incorrect_recovery_sequencing: Bending the knees before the hands have cleared them on the recovery, which creates a collision where the handle must travel over or around the knees. The correct recovery sequence is strictly: arms extend first, then the body swings forward, then the knees bend to slide the seat up. Breaking this sequence compresses the stroke and prevents the athlete from reaching a proper catch position.
common_errors.over_compression_at_catch: Sliding so far forward that the seat nearly touches the heels, the shins travel well past vertical, and the lower back rounds under load — this is a mechanically weak position from which minimal force can be generated on the initial drive. The shins should be vertical at the catch, the shoulders should be just in front of the hips, and the core should be braced and loaded ready to transmit leg force.
common_errors.excessive_layback_at_finish: Leaning far past 30 degrees behind vertical at the finish of the stroke does not add power and creates a longer, slower recovery that disrupts stroke rhythm and timing. A finish position of approximately 25–30 degrees of lean with a braced core and handle drawn to the lower sternum is mechanically efficient; going further is wasted motion that coaches actively train athletes out of.
common_errors.rushing_the_slide: Allowing the seat to slide forward quickly during recovery rather than maintaining a controlled 1:2 drive-to-recovery ratio — this disrupts timing, prevents the muscles from recovering between strokes, and reduces the quality of each subsequent drive. The drive should be explosive and hard; the recovery should be deliberate and slow, allowing the body to reset before the next catch.
common_errors.feet_too_high_in_foot_stretcher: Placing the foot strap across the arch or midfoot rather than across the widest part of the foot at the toes reduces the range of forward lean available at the catch, limiting the athlete's ability to load the posterior chain before the drive. The strap should sit across the ball of the foot so that the heel can rise freely and full forward compression can be achieved.

common_errors.early_back_rounding: Allowing the thoracic spine to flex excessively when hugging the bag rather than maintaining a braced, upright posture — the shifting load of a sandbag makes spinal position more difficult to sustain than with rigid implements, and a rounded back places the erectors in a mechanically weak position under load.
common_errors.bag_drifting_away_from_torso: Letting the sandbag drop down and away from the chest rather than keeping it high and tight — distance from the center of mass increases the moment arm and dramatically elevates the effective load on the lower back. The cue is to actively squeeze the bag into the sternum throughout the carry.
common_errors.inadequate_bracing_with_breathing: Releasing intra-abdominal pressure entirely to take a breath, particularly noticeable because the bag presses directly on the chest and makes deep breathing difficult. Athletes must learn to take short diaphragmatic breaths without fully dropping core tension, or fatigue will manifest as back breakdown long before the legs or grip fail.
common_errors.wrong_grip_position: Placing hands directly under the bag rather than around the sides with forearms framing the load — underhand positioning forces the biceps to carry the majority of the load, increasing the risk of bicipital strain, one of the most commonly reported sandbag carry injuries.

common_errors.elbow_bending: Bending the elbows during the retraction phase turns the exercise into a mini pull-up, recruiting the biceps and lats as primary movers and bypassing the scapular stabilizers that are the entire training target. The elbows must remain nearly locked straight and movement occurs only at the shoulder blade.
common_errors.insufficient_depression: Going through the motions without fully depressing the scapulae — just twitching them slightly — provides no useful training stimulus. The shoulder blades must travel their full range from the elevated passive hang position to maximum depression, and the body should visibly rise a few inches.
common_errors.no_pause_at_top: Failing to pause in the fully depressed position eliminates the isometric hold that trains endurance and neuromuscular awareness of the depressed scapular position — exactly the position that is required at the initiation of every pull-up.
common_errors.swinging: Allowing the body to swing forward and backward introduces momentum that reduces the scapular isolation and can destabilize the shoulder joint. The core must be braced and the body kept still throughout.
common_errors.skipping_the_exercise: Athletes who have never practiced this isolation often begin full pull-ups with passively elevated scapulae, which is a leading contributor to shoulder impingement and long head bicep tendon irritation. This exercise should be mastered before progressing to full pull-ups.

common_errors.lumbar_rounding_and_forward_lean: Collapsing the torso forward on the eccentric and then throwing it back on the concentric — this momentum-based pattern offloads the target musculature and places cyclic flexion-extension stress on the lumbar discs. The torso should remain near-vertical with a slight fixed forward lean maintained isometrically throughout.
common_errors.using_arms_before_scapulae: Initiating the pull with elbow flexion before the scapulae have begun retracting — the correct sequence is scapular retraction first, then elbow drive, then full contraction. Starting with the arms bypasses the mid-trap and rhomboid stimulus entirely.
common_errors.insufficient_full_contraction: Stopping the pull before the elbows have traveled fully past the torso — the rhomboids and middle trapezius only reach their peak activation in the last quarter of the movement, so abbreviated reps systematically under-train the intended muscles.
common_errors.protracted_scapulae_at_start: Not allowing the shoulder blades to fully protract on the eccentric — while controlled, full protraction at the start of each rep is what ensures the serratus anterior, mid-trap, and rhomboids are trained through their full range rather than only their shortened position.
common_errors.grip_attachment_ignored: Using the same attachment regardless of training goal — close neutral grip maximizes lat activation, wide pronated grip shifts emphasis to upper back and rear deltoids. Coaches should prescribe attachment based on which muscles need development, not default to whichever is already on the machine.

common_errors.elbow_bending: Bending the elbow at the end of the punch converts a pure scapular protraction exercise into a pressing movement dominated by the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid. The arm must remain nearly straight throughout, and the movement comes from the shoulder blade protracting forward around the ribcage — not the elbow extending.
common_errors.no_end_range_protraction: Stopping the movement before maximal scapular protraction is reached eliminates the primary training stimulus — the serratus is most active in the last few degrees of forward reach where the scapula wraps forward around the rib cage. The athlete should consciously push the shoulder blade as far forward as possible at end range.
common_errors.trunk_rotation: Rotating the trunk to follow the arm instead of isolating the scapulothoracic joint substitutes spinal mobility for the scapular mobility and strength the exercise is designed to train. The torso must remain square and still, with only the shoulder blade moving.
common_errors.pec_minor_dominance: In patients with a tight or dominant pectoralis minor, the scapula anteriorly tilts instead of protracting — this looks similar to but is biomechanically opposite to correct serratus activation. Cue the athlete to reach forward through the shoulder blade rather than rolling it forward, and monitor for anterior shoulder tipping.
common_errors.insufficient_load: Performing the exercise with no resistance or negligible resistance at very high reps produces neuromuscular activation training but does not build the endurance capacity needed for overhead athletes. Once the movement pattern is established, progressing load via cable or band resistance is necessary to develop functional serratus strength.

common_errors.hip_drop: Allowing the hips to sag toward the floor rather than keeping them elevated in a straight line — the most common and most consequential error. This eliminates the lateral anti-flexion demand entirely and is functionally equivalent to not doing the exercise.
common_errors.forward_hip_rotation: Letting the top hip rotate forward so the pelvis is no longer perpendicular to the floor. This shifts the load away from the lateral stabilizers and into the hip flexors and lumbar extensors, defeating the anti-rotation purpose of the drill.
common_errors.shoulder_collapse: Sinking into the supporting shoulder rather than actively pushing the floor away to create space. This impinges the shoulder, removes the serratus anterior from the co-contraction pattern, and creates a shearing force at the glenohumeral joint over time.
common_errors.neck_deviation: Looking up at the ceiling or dropping the head toward the floor instead of maintaining neutral cervical alignment. The neck should follow the same straight-line body position from ears to feet.
common_errors.too_wide_foot_stance: Staggering the feet front-to-back to gain a more stable base rather than stacking them. This wider base reduces the lateral core challenge and is a subtle but common cheat that disguises itself as good form.

common_errors.using_the_opposite_leg_to_assist: Toe-tapping or bearing weight through the non-working foot during the concentric phase, effectively converting a unilateral exercise into a bilateral one and masking the strength deficit the exercise is prescribed to address — this is especially common in Achilles tendinopathy rehab where pain limits the working leg's effort.
common_errors.insufficient_range_of_motion: Not dorsiflexing fully at the bottom of each rep, particularly when performed on a step or decline board. The Achilles and gastrocnemius-soleus complex must be adequately lengthened to generate the therapeutic tendon loading prescribed in protocols like the Alfredson eccentric heel drop.
common_errors.swinging_the_free_leg: Using momentum from the non-working leg to assist the lift, particularly when fatigued. The non-working leg should be held in a consistent position, often with the knee bent, and should contribute nothing to the upward movement.
common_errors.excessively_fast_concentric: Performing the up-phase too quickly, which sacrifices motor control and reduces the muscle activation compared to a controlled 2-second concentric. Single-leg calf raises in rehabilitation contexts should maintain consistent tempo throughout both phases.
common_errors.not_controlling_ankle_eversion_or_invers: Allowing the ankle to roll outward (supination) or inward (pronation) during the raise, which indicates insufficient ankle stability and transfers load unevenly across the Achilles insertion and plantar fascia. The heel should travel straight up and straight down throughout the movement.

common_errors.hip_asymmetry: Allowing the hips to rise unevenly — the non-working hip drops toward the floor as the working glute extends, which indicates the hip abductors of the stance leg cannot maintain pelvic stability during the unilateral demand and represents a significant bilateral imbalance worth addressing.
common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension_at_lockout: Arching the lower back aggressively at the top of the movement instead of achieving posterior pelvic tilt — the finish position should show a straight line from knee to shoulder with no excessive lumbar curve; hyperextension shifts load to the erectors and lumbar facets rather than peaking glute activation.
common_errors.insufficient_proficiency_to_progress: Moving to single-leg hip thrusts before achieving bilateral hip thrust competency and single-leg glute bridge baseline — the increased stability demand and range of motion means compensatory patterns (lateral trunk sway, foot scrabbling) will dominate if the prerequisite strength base is not in place.
common_errors.foot_position: Placing the working foot too close to or too far from the hips changes the muscle emphasis considerably; too close reduces hamstring contribution and increases quad demand, while too far increases hamstring contribution but reduces peak glute activation — a position where the shin is roughly vertical at the top is generally optimal for glute emphasis.
common_errors.losing_upper_back_contact: Allowing the bench contact point to slide or the upper back to round off the edge reduces the ROM advantage that separates the hip thrust from the floor glute bridge, diminishing both glute stretch at the bottom and the ability to achieve full hip extension at the top.

common_errors.hip_rotation_opening: The hip of the elevated leg rotating outward — so the pelvis tilts and one hip rises higher than the other — is the most pervasive error in the SLRDL and directly limits hamstring loading on the working leg. The pelvis must remain squared to the floor throughout the hinge; cue 'keep both hip bones pointing down to the ground' or use a dowel across the pelvis as a feedback tool.
common_errors.rounded_lumbar_spine: Losing spinal neutrality as the torso descends removes the isometric back-extension demand from the movement and transfers the load to passive lumbar structures. The erectors must stay actively engaged in a neutral or slightly extended position; if the back rounds before a meaningful hamstring stretch is achieved, the weight is too heavy or the athlete needs bilateral RDL regression first.
common_errors.standing_knee_hyperextension: Locking out the standing knee removes the slight eccentric hamstring co-contraction that controls pelvic position and distributes load to the knee joint itself in a non-ideal range. A 10–15 degree soft bend in the standing knee is mandatory for proper mechanics and injury prevention.
common_errors.using_momentum_to_return: Swinging the rear leg back to the standing position rather than using a deliberate hip extension contraction makes the eccentric phase — which carries the bulk of the injury-preventive and strength-building stimulus — entirely passive. Every rep should include a 2-3 second controlled descent and a deliberate concentric drive through the glute and hamstring of the working leg.
common_errors.too_much_knee_bend: Compensating for limited hamstring flexibility by excessively flexing the standing knee converts the movement into a single-leg squat rather than a hip hinge, significantly reducing the hamstring stimulus. The shin of the working leg should remain mostly vertical and the movement should be felt predominantly in the posterior thigh, not the quad.

common_errors.knee_anterior_to_toes: Allowing the knee of the working leg to slide forward past the foot, which shifts load onto the patellar tendon and patellofemoral joint. In a true wall sit, the shin should be roughly vertical with the knee tracking over the toes — any excessive forward knee travel defeats the knee-friendly design of the exercise.
common_errors.collapsing_below_90_degrees: Sinking the hips below parallel, which dramatically increases patellofemoral joint compressive forces. For most rehab applications, a 90-degree hip and knee angle is the target — going lower should only be programmed when the athlete has demonstrated tolerance.
common_errors.losing_lumbar_contact_with_wall: Allowing the lower back to peel away from the wall, usually as fatigue develops, which introduces spinal load and signals that form has broken down. The entire spine should remain in contact with the wall throughout the hold.
common_errors.excessive_hip_flexor_compensation: Raising the free leg too high or using strong hip flexor contraction on the elevated leg to help stabilize the position rather than relying on the stance leg quadriceps and glutes. The free leg should be held at a comfortable height, typically with the thigh parallel to the floor.
common_errors.breath_holding: Performing a Valsalva maneuver during the isometric hold, which dangerously elevates blood pressure. Athletes should breathe continuously throughout the hold, particularly relevant for older populations and those with cardiovascular risk factors using this exercise in rehab protocols.

common_errors.elbow_initiating_instead_of_lat: Pulling by leading with the hand and flexing the elbow first rather than retracting the scapula and driving the elbow up and back — this turns the row into a biceps-dominant movement. Cue: think of the hand as a hook and the elbow as the engine.
common_errors.excessive_trunk_rotation: Rotating the torso during the concentric to gain additional range of motion — while a small degree of rotation is acceptable in Kroc-style rows, excessive rotation in a standard single-arm row reduces lat isolation and transfers load to the spinal rotators, changing the exercise character entirely.
common_errors.rounding_of_the_non-working_side: Collapsing the supporting shoulder and side, causing the spine to laterally flex toward the floor — the non-working arm and leg must maintain rigid structural support so the entire spinal and trunk load is stable before the working arm initiates.
common_errors.pulling_height_too_low: Stopping the elbow at torso level rather than driving it above the back — at the top position the elbow should travel past the line of the spine to achieve full rhomboid and middle trap contraction. Low pulls bias the lats while leaving the upper back undertrained.
common_errors.not_setting_neutral_spine_first: Starting each rep from a rounded back because the setup on the bench was rushed — the athlete must establish lumbar neutrality and brace the core before the rep begins, not attempt to correct it mid-pull.

common_errors.hip_drop_on_free_side: The non-working side hip drooping toward the floor during the lift — indicates gluteus medius weakness on the stance side and puts the pelvis into lateral tilt. This is a critical dysfunction to correct before loading the movement.
common_errors.hip_rotation: The pelvis rotating toward the non-working leg, rather than staying square — often masked by athletes rushing through reps. Rotation de-loads the working glute and creates asymmetrical forces on the SI joint.
common_errors.lumbar_hyperextension: Arching the lower back instead of posteriorly tilting the pelvis at lockout, particularly common when fatigued. The free-leg position amplifies this tendency when athletes try to compensate for reduced stability.
common_errors.insufficient_range_of_motion: Not reaching full hip extension at the top, often because the athlete is balancing rather than driving. Full extension is required for peak gluteus maximus activation — partial reps miss the peak contraction.
common_errors.free_leg_instability: Using the non-working leg as a counterbalance by swinging it or pressing it into the floor mid-rep, which reduces the unilateral demand. The free leg should stay consistent — either bent in the air or extended, without dynamic compensation.

common_errors.elbows_flaring_wide: Allowing the elbows to splay outward during the descent turns the movement into a partial floor press, recruiting the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid to assist and completely changing the loading pattern from triceps isolation to multi-joint pressing. Elbows must track narrow and forward.
common_errors.upper_arms_moving: Allowing the upper arms to travel backward toward the head during the descent (instead of keeping them slightly angled and stationary) converts the skull crusher into a pullover motion and removes the eccentric loading from the triceps. The humeral angle should be fixed throughout each rep.
common_errors.dropping_the_bar_rapidly: Gravity-assisted descent onto the forehead is where the exercise got its name — and where the injury risk lives. Uncontrolled eccentric loading at the elbow joint accumulates stress on the olecranon and distal triceps tendon and is the primary cause of elbow pain from this exercise.
common_errors.locking_out_at_the_top: Fully locking out the elbows directly over the face brings the forearm vertical and removes all tension from the triceps at the top. Coaches cue lifters to stop extension just short of lockout with the arms angled slightly back to maintain continuous triceps loading throughout the set.
common_errors.excessive_load_causing_wrist_breakdown: Overloading with a straight bar forces the wrists into maximal pronation and can cause medial wrist and elbow pain over time. Switching to an EZ-bar or dumbbells at heavy loads reduces wrist deviation and is a standard sports medicine recommendation for athletes with elbow complaints.

common_errors.passive_arm_pulling: Using only the arm muscles to drag the sled forward rather than driving with hip extension and leg push — the primary force should come from the lower body, with the arms serving as the connection point. Athletes who fatigue their arms before their legs are not driving through the hips.
common_errors.leaning_excessively_backward: Leaning far back during a backward pull drag to increase leverage, which places the lumbar spine in hyperextension under load. A slight backward lean is appropriate; aggressive backward trunk positioning compresses the lumbar facet joints and removes gluteal drive from the movement.
common_errors.loss_of_knee_flexion: Walking with straight legs during a backward drag, which reduces hamstring engagement and forces the load onto the lower back. A slight knee bend on every step keeps the posterior chain under tension and reduces spinal compressive stress.
common_errors.inconsistent_pace: Stopping and starting repeatedly rather than maintaining steady continuous tension. For conditioning, consistent tension produces superior metabolic demand; for strength, the pause-and-restart creates much higher peak force demands that are appropriate only for heavy, short-distance pulls.

common_errors.upright_torso: Pushing with an excessively upright trunk instead of leaning the body forward at roughly 45 degrees reduces horizontal force application and makes the athlete work against gravity rather than with it. An upright position dramatically cuts the effective power transferred to the sled and shifts effort toward the arms rather than the legs.
common_errors.too_heavy_too_slow: Loading the sled so heavy that it barely moves produces a grinding eccentric-absent stimulus but eliminates the power and acceleration training benefit. Heavy sleds (>80% load) have their place for pure strength, but most athletes default to maximal loads when moderate loads at higher velocity produce superior rate-of-force-development adaptations.
common_errors.heel_striking: Pushing off the heel rather than the ball of the foot — the sled push demands a forefoot strike and calf drive to complete each step, and heel-dominant athletes lose significant force transmission at the terminal push phase. Some elite coaches cue athletes to never let the heel touch the ground throughout the set.
common_errors.quitting_on_deceleration: Stopping when the sled slows rather than when the prescribed distance is covered. The slow, grinding portion when fatigue accumulates is where the metabolic and neuromuscular adaptations are highest — terminating early consistently removes the most valuable portion of the set.

common_errors.hips_rising_faster_than_shoulders: Because the snatch pull starts from a lower hip position and wider grip than the clean pull, athletes are especially prone to letting the hips rise first, converting the movement into a good morning before the second pull and losing the vertical drive angle needed to send the bar overhead.
common_errors.insufficient_back_angle_hold: Allowing the torso angle to change rapidly in the first pull before the bar clears the knees breaks the continuous tension on the hamstrings; the back angle should remain nearly constant from floor to just above knee level.
common_errors.over_reliance_on_shrug_not_extension: Emphasizing the trapezius shrug while under-driving with the legs produces a bar path that peaks low and far forward — the shrug should be a consequence of full hip and knee extension, not a substitute for it.
common_errors.loading_too_heavy: Because the snatch pull can be trained at 85-115% of one's snatch, athletes often load it so heavy that bar path mechanics deteriorate, programming a slow or compromised second pull rather than reinforcing the speed demanded by competition snatches.
common_errors.elbows_bending_during_extension: Beginning to flex the elbows as the bar reaches the hip rather than maintaining long straight arms for the full duration of the pull; any early elbow bend leaks force out of the system and reduces bar velocity before the turnover phase.

common_errors.knee_drift_forward: Allowing the knees to travel forward over the toes during the squat, which reintroduces the patellofemoral compressive forces the exercise is specifically designed to eliminate. The shin must remain as vertical as possible throughout — the whole purpose of the band is to allow a vertical tibia by counterbalancing the torso backward.
common_errors.insufficient_band_tension: Using a band that is too light or not stepping far enough from the anchor point, so the band fails to adequately support the posterior lean and the athlete defaults to a standard squat pattern with knee drift. The band should create enough tension that the athlete can sit upright with shins nearly vertical.
common_errors.excessive_depth: Squatting well below 90 degrees of knee flexion, which re-loads the patellar tendon and patellofemoral joint beyond the therapeutic range. Most patellar tendinopathy protocols target a thigh-parallel position; going lower provides diminishing returns and increases the risk of a symptom flare.
common_errors.hip_flexion: Folding at the hips or allowing the trunk to lean forward rather than staying tall, which shifts load from the quadriceps onto the posterior chain and negates the exercise's targeted quad tendon loading effect. The torso should remain upright or slightly reclined throughout.
common_errors.insufficient_hold_duration: Rushing through reps rather than holding the isometric position for the prescribed time (typically 30–45 seconds per set). The analgesic and tendon-loading benefits of the Spanish Squat are directly tied to sustained isometric tension — quick reps produce little of the intended effect.

common_errors.upper_arms_not_vertical: Allowing the upper arms to swing backward (toward the bench) as the weight is lowered rather than keeping them vertical and perpendicular to the floor. The defining biomechanical feature of the spider curl is that the resistance arm is longest at the top (full elbow flexion), providing peak contraction overload; if the upper arm drifts back the overload shifts to mid-range and the exercise degrades toward a standard curl.
common_errors.losing_tension_at_bottom: Lowering the weight so far that the elbows lock out and the biceps go slack at full extension. Unlike the incline curl where the full stretch is the goal, the spider curl is optimized for top-of-range tension; full lockout with dangling arms at the bottom removes the constant tension advantage.
common_errors.using_momentum: Swinging the weight up by recruiting the posterior deltoid or using body movement to initiate the curl. The prone position is supposed to eliminate this entirely — if swinging is still occurring the load is too heavy.
common_errors.too_steep_a_bench_angle: Setting the bench at 70–80° (almost vertical) rather than approximately 45°. Very steep angles shift the arm position closer to a preacher curl setup, reducing the range where the biceps are maximally loaded. Approximately 45° provides the optimal combination of arm verticality and braced chest support.

common_errors.front_shin_not_vertical: Allowing the front knee to travel far over the toes or, conversely, keeping it too far back both shift the loading away from the intended muscles. Excessive forward travel amplifies patellofemoral compressive forces; insufficient forward travel removes quad contribution and turns the exercise into a hip-dominant hinge. The front shin should be roughly vertical at the bottom and the lifter should feel the quad working throughout.
common_errors.back_knee_slamming_floor: Dropping the rear knee to the floor without eccentric control develops no negative-phase strength, produces shock loading on the rear knee, and trains a sloppy movement pattern. The descent should be controlled and deliberate; a 2-count eccentric is the minimum coaching standard.
common_errors.weight_distribution_on_back_foot: Leaning back or bearing excessive weight through the rear foot turns the exercise bilateral and defeats its purpose as a unilateral strength test. Roughly 80–90% of force production should originate from the front leg; if the lifter cannot maintain this, the load is too heavy or the hip flexors are too tight to allow a proper front-leg-dominated position.
common_errors.valgus_knee_collapse: The front knee caving inward during the ascent is identical in mechanism and consequence to valgus collapse in a squat — hip abductor weakness plus lack of cued external rotation. In the split squat it tends to appear under fatigue or at the end of a set, making it essential for coaches to monitor rep quality throughout rather than just the first rep.
common_errors.trunk_rotation: The shoulders and hips rotating away from square during the movement is a form of lateral stability compensation and indicates either hip tightness or unilateral trunk weakness. It introduces rotational shear into the hip and lumbar spine that accumulates into injury; a dowel held across the shoulders is a useful diagnostic and correction tool.

common_errors.poor_arm_swing: Not using a full countermovement arm swing — research confirms arm swing contributes meaningfully to horizontal distance by transferring momentum and increasing the vertical force component at takeoff. Arms should swing aggressively back and then explosively forward.
common_errors.incomplete_hip_loading: Not loading into a sufficient countermovement squat before takeoff — athletes who barely dip lose elastic energy storage and produce a purely concentric jump, which underperforms a stretch-shortening cycle jump by 10–15%.
common_errors.upright_torso_at_takeoff: Maintaining too vertical a torso instead of leaning forward through the hips at takeoff — an anterior trunk lean of roughly 45 degrees maximizes horizontal projection angle and shifts force application direction appropriately.
common_errors.collapsing_on_landing: Landing with the hips dropping far behind the heels, which reduces jump distance and places excessive stress on the knee joint. Athletes should pull the thighs toward the chest in late flight and actively reach the feet forward while keeping the center of mass over the base.
common_errors.bilateral_asymmetry: Dominant-leg loading at takeoff creates asymmetrical ground reaction forces — relevant in assessment contexts where bilateral power discrepancies indicate injury risk and should be flagged for follow-up.

common_errors.insufficient_range_of_motion: Not achieving full plantar flexion at the top of the rep, leaving the calf in a shortened position and forfeiting the greatest muscle activation and hypertrophic stimulus. At the top the heel should be as high as the ankle anatomy allows, ideally with a visible peak contraction pause.
common_errors.bouncing_at_the_bottom: Using a rapid stretch reflex at the bottom rather than achieving a controlled dorsiflexion before each rep, which reduces time under tension in the stretched position. Research shows standing calf raises performed at long muscle lengths (deep dorsiflexion on a step) produce substantially greater gastrocnemius hypertrophy.
common_errors.bent_knee: Allowing a significant knee bend during the exercise, which places the gastrocnemius in active insufficiency and shifts the load almost entirely to the soleus. A standing calf raise with the knee straight is required to maximally load the biarticular gastrocnemius.
common_errors.uncontrolled_descent: Dropping the heels rapidly on the eccentric rather than lowering them slowly under control. The eccentric phase of calf training is particularly important for Achilles tendon health and hypertrophy — a 3-second lowering cadence is recommended by most sports medicine protocols for Achilles rehabilitation.
common_errors.excessive_external_rotation: Turning the feet out significantly to bias the medial gastrocnemius, or internally rotating to bias the lateral head, when the goal is general strength development. A neutral or very slight outward toe position is appropriate for most athletes; exaggerated rotations add asymmetrical stress to the Achilles tendon.

common_errors.knee_valgus: Allowing the knee of the standing leg to cave inward (medial collapse) during the descent, which is a hallmark sign of insufficient gluteus medius and hip abductor strength and dramatically increases patellofemoral stress and ACL loading. The knee should track in line with the second toe throughout the entire lowering phase.
common_errors.rushing_the_descent: Dropping the non-weight-bearing leg quickly rather than controlling the lowering over 3–5 seconds. The entire therapeutic purpose of this exercise is the controlled eccentric quadriceps contraction — a fast descent removes this stimulus entirely and converts the exercise into a balance drill.
common_errors.contralateral_hip_drop: Allowing the pelvis to tilt downward on the side of the lowering leg (Trendelenburg pattern), indicating weak ipsilateral hip abductors. This is both a sign of dysfunction to be corrected and a compensatory pattern that must be actively cued against.
common_errors.pushing_off_with_the_free_foot: Making contact with the floor and loading the non-standing leg to assist the return to the start position, effectively converting the unilateral exercise into a bilateral one and masking the strength deficit being targeted. The free foot should only lightly tap the floor.
common_errors.using_a_box_that_is_too_high: Selecting a step height beyond what the athlete can control through the full range of motion, resulting in loss of eccentric control in the mid-to-end range where quad demand is highest. Step height should be limited to a height that allows a smooth, controlled descent from start to heel tap.

common_errors.pushing_off_the_back_foot: Toeing off the back foot to drive the body up is the most common error in the step-up and completely offloads the working leg, converting a unilateral exercise into a disguised bilateral push. The entire propulsive force must come from the heel of the elevated foot; the back foot should be lifted immediately after the step, not used as a launching platform.
common_errors.box_too_low: A box height below knee height dramatically reduces hip extension range of motion, limiting glute and hamstring recruitment. The standard coaching recommendation is a box at or near knee height, which forces the working hip to travel through a meaningful range and creates the posterior chain loading that justifies programming the exercise.
common_errors.forward_torso_lean: Excessive forward lean shifts the center of mass forward and reduces the glute loading by moving hip extension moment arm — it mirrors the forward lean error in a split squat and often signals quad weakness or limited ankle dorsiflexion. The torso should remain upright with the weight driving through the heel.
common_errors.uncontrolled_descent: Dropping the rear leg back to the floor rather than controlling the eccentric reduces time under tension and eliminates much of the hypertrophic stimulus. Elite coaches program the step-down as deliberately as the step-up, either with a controlled negative or a pause at the top before lowering.
common_errors.asymmetrical_hip_drop: The hip of the non-working leg hiking upward during the ascent is a sign of gluteus medius weakness on the working side and creates lateral pelvic tilt under load. This pattern is common and important to flag because it indicates a unilateral hip stability deficit with direct implications for running mechanics and knee injury risk.

common_errors.lateral_trunk_lean: Allowing the torso to lean toward the weighted side rather than staying perfectly upright — this collapses the anti-lateral flexion challenge entirely and turns the exercise into a loaded side bend, defeating its purpose and increasing compressive load on the lumbar spine.
common_errors.loaded_shoulder_elevation: The shoulder holding the weight frequently rides up as fatigue sets in, causing the trap to shorten instead of stabilize. The coaching cue is to actively depress the loaded shoulder, keeping it level with the unloaded side throughout the walk.
common_errors.core_disengagement_between_steps: Athletes brace hard during the initial pick-up but relax the core during walking, allowing rhythmic lateral trunk shifts with each step. McGill's research on suitcase carry specifically highlights that the quadratus lumborum must maintain continuous tension to stiffen the pelvis and resist lateral bend during the swing phase.
common_errors.asymmetric_volume: Performing more distance or reps on the stronger side — since the exercise exists specifically to address bilateral imbalances, the weaker side must be matched and never skipped, or imbalances will be reinforced rather than corrected.

common_errors.lateral_trunk_bend_toward_weight: Leaning toward the loaded side as the weight is lifted — this is the most critical fault, as the entire training stimulus of the suitcase deadlift is the anti-lateral flexion demand placed on the contralateral obliques and QL; any side-bend collapses that demand and loads the ipsilateral spine passively instead.
common_errors.shoulder_elevation_on_loaded_side: Shrugging or hiking the shoulder on the hand holding the weight shifts the load from the hip hinge mechanics to the trapezius and elevators, changing the nature of the exercise from a deadlift into an asymmetric carry — the shoulder must actively be packed down throughout.
common_errors.hips_not_square_at_lockout: Allowing one hip to hike higher than the other during the lift or at the top position indicates the hip abductors are not isometrically maintaining pelvic level, which is a fundamental purpose of this exercise — hips must be even from floor to standing.
common_errors.treating_it_like_a_regular_deadlift: Performing the movement focused on hip extension output rather than treating the anti-lateral-flexion demand as the primary training goal — the weight should be light enough to maintain perfect symmetry throughout, not maximized for hip extension load; when the load gets heavy, spinal neutrality is typically the first thing lost.
common_errors.foot_and_bar_placement: Placing the weight in front of or behind the foot rather than directly beside it (lined up with mid-foot laterally) changes the pull vector and makes maintaining a neutral spine through the hinge substantially harder — precise lateral setup is what makes the load feel manageable and sustainable.

common_errors.hips_rising_first: The hips shooting up before the bar breaks the floor turns the lift into a stiff-leg deadlift with a wide stance and removes the quad contribution entirely — the very mechanical advantage that defines sumo's setup. The knees and hips must extend simultaneously; coaches cue 'push the floor away' or 'leg press the bar up' to keep the torso angle constant off the floor.
common_errors.toes_not_sufficiently_turned_out: Feet that are not flared outward enough relative to the lifter's hip anatomy create a mechanical conflict where the femurs collide with the pelvis before reaching optimal depth. The toes must point in the same direction as the knees throughout the lift; the exact angle varies by individual hip structure and must be found through setup experimentation.
common_errors.knees_caving_inward: Valgus collapse during the ascent is especially dangerous in sumo because the wide stance places the adductors and hip abductors in a mechanically demanding position — knees collapsing inward creates high shear load across the medial knee. The lifter must actively externally rotate the femurs, tracking knees over toes.
common_errors.hips_too_far_from_bar: Setting up with the hips too far back from the bar lengthens the moment arm and essentially converts the sumo into a conventional pull, eliminating the upright torso advantage. In sumo, the bar should be almost directly below the shoulder joint at setup, with shins close to vertical.
common_errors.lumbar_flexion_at_lockout: Rounding the lower back at the top of the pull — especially common when overloaded — increases compressive and shear forces on the intervertebral discs well beyond safe margins. The pelvis should remain in neutral or slight posterior tilt as the hips drive forward to lockout; hyperextending the lumbar spine to 'finish' the rep is equally problematic.

common_errors.lumbar_rounding_under_load: Allowing the lower back to flex during the pull, especially as fatigue accumulates — T-bar row loads a forward-hinged torso under heavy compression and the lumbar spine must be locked into neutral with a braced core before the bar moves. Lumbar flexion here is among the highest-risk errors in any row variation.
common_errors.torso_too_upright: Standing with excessive trunk elevation rather than maintaining a torso angle of approximately 45° to the floor — an upright torso converts the T-bar row into a shrug and trap-dominant pull rather than a lat and mid-back row. The forward lean is what creates the horizontal pull vector.
common_errors.arm_dominance_over_back_drive: Initiating the pull by flexing the elbows rather than first retracting the scapulae and driving the elbows toward the hips — identical to the barbell row error; the arms should function as load-bearing links, not motors. Athletes who feel the exercise primarily in the biceps are almost always initiating incorrectly.
common_errors.leg_drive_momentum: Using a small leg push or hip thrust at the bottom of each rep to break the weight free — this is particularly common with heavier loads and effectively converts the top portion of the rep into a momentum-driven movement with minimal back activation. The bar should be pulled purely with upper back musculature from a static hip-hinge position.
common_errors.attachment_handle_ignored: Using whatever handle is already attached rather than selecting based on training priority — V-handle (neutral close grip) emphasizes lat thickness and allows maximum load; wide pronated handle shifts emphasis to upper back and rear deltoids with reduced elbow joint stress. Coaches should prescribe the attachment that matches the athlete's specific development need.

common_errors.insufficient_quad_contraction: Going through the motion without actively squeezing the quadriceps to a full terminal lock-out, which defeats the primary purpose of VMO recruitment. The athlete should feel a firm contraction at the point of full extension and hold briefly — the cue 'squeeze like you're cracking a nut with your knee' is commonly used.
common_errors.hyperextending_the_knee: Pushing the knee so far back into extension that it recurves past neutral, which can irritate the posterior capsule and is especially dangerous post-ACL reconstruction. The goal is firm, active extension to neutral — not passive sag into hyperextension.
common_errors.band_positioned_too_low: Anchoring or positioning the band below the knee rather than directly behind it at joint level, which changes the lever arm and direction of resistance, reducing the specificity of the exercise for terminal extension and transferring load away from the VMO.
common_errors.compensating_with_hip_extension: Driving the hip into extension to assist the knee straightening, which is a subtle compensation that unloads the quadriceps. The torso should remain upright and the movement should be isolated to the last 30 degrees of knee extension against the band.
common_errors.moving_too_fast: Performing reps quickly without pausing at full extension, missing the key neuromuscular re-education goal of the exercise. After surgical knee procedures, TKEs are prescribed to restore active terminal extension and neuromuscular control — tempo and contraction quality matter far more than speed or load.

common_errors.partial_range_of_motion: Not fully dorsiflexing the ankle (pulling toes as far toward the shin as possible) at the top, which limits the peak contraction of the tibialis anterior. The goal is maximum dorsiflexion — athletes should feel a strong burn in the shin at the top of every rep.
common_errors.no_controlled_lowering: Dropping the foot back to the starting position rather than slowly returning under control. The eccentric phase is equally important for building tibialis anterior strength and length, and fast returns reduce the training stimulus by roughly half.
common_errors.not_standing_far_enough_from_wall: In the wall variation, standing too close eliminates the load-bearing angle and makes the exercise nearly effortless, providing insufficient resistance for a training effect. As a rule of thumb, the exercise should become meaningfully challenging by rep 10–15 at the chosen foot position.
common_errors.using_hip_flexion_to_assist: Lifting the entire leg or flexing at the hip to help bring the foot up, rather than isolating the movement to ankle dorsiflexion. This compensation is especially common in athletes with a weak tibialis anterior — the knee and hip should remain stationary throughout.
common_errors.neglecting_progressive_overload: Staying with bodyweight or a light band indefinitely once the exercise becomes easy, when a tib bar or heavier resistance would produce far greater strength and hypertrophy adaptations. The tibialis anterior responds well to heavier loading and progressing from wall raises to loaded tib bar raises is the standard progression.

common_errors.starting_too_close_to_tire: Setting up with the toes directly under the tire bottom edge prevents generating a horizontal pulling angle during the first pull phase and forces a straight-up deadlift-style pull. The optimal start position has the feet slightly back from the tire so the pull trajectory angles the tire forward rather than straight up, allowing momentum to carry it through the transition.
common_errors.no_transition_grip_change: Failing to switch from an underhand 'scooping' grip to an overhand push grip as the tire rises to chest height — athletes who skip this transition must muscle the tire the entire way with arms instead of explosively pushing through, dramatically reducing how heavy a tire they can flip and increasing bicep strain risk.
common_errors.hip_extension_timing_error: Pulling with the back before the hips have extended — the sequence must be legs first, then hip drive, then back, mirroring a power clean. Initiating with the back bypasses the most powerful muscles in the chain and places extreme shear load on the lumbar spine in a flexed position.
common_errors.standing_upright_too_early: Extending to full upright posture when the tire is only halfway up, which removes horizontal force production exactly when it is most needed for the push-over phase. Athletes should maintain forward lean and drive horizontally into the tire until it passes the tipping point.
common_errors.dropping_hips_late: In competition-style flipping for reps, re-approaching the tire with hips high and driving it with the back rather than resquatting for each rep — this is a common fatigue-related error that compounds spinal load with every subsequent repetition.

common_errors.hips_shooting_up: The hips rising faster than the shoulders — identical to the same error in the conventional deadlift — converts the lift into a stiff-leg pull and removes the quad contribution that is the primary reason to choose the trap bar over a straight bar. The lifter should think of it as a leg press against the floor, extending knees and hips simultaneously.
common_errors.using_low_handles_prematurely: Beginners defaulting to low handles before they have the hip mobility and posterior chain strength to maintain a flat back at that depth frequently lose spinal neutrality at the bottom, loading the lumbar spine in flexion under heavy load. High handles reduce range of motion and allow proper bracing to be established first.
common_errors.overextending_at_lockout: Leaning back aggressively at the top to complete the rep hyperloads the lumbar extensors and is not a display of strength — it is compensation for inadequate hip drive. The endpoint is standing tall with hips fully extended and glutes contracted, not arching backward.
common_errors.bar_drifting_forward: Because the handles sit at the sides of the body, inexperienced lifters sometimes allow the bar to drift forward during the ascent, shifting the load to the toes and increasing lower back moment. The bar should track vertically over the mid-foot throughout, with the lats actively pulling the handles back toward the hips.
common_errors.insufficient_lat_engagement: Failing to brace the lats before pulling allows the shoulders to roll forward and the upper back to round under load. The cue 'protect your armpits' or 'bend the bar around your legs' engages the lats, sets the shoulder blades, and creates the rigid torso necessary for safe heavy loading.

common_errors.excessive_load: Using too much weight eliminates the ability to achieve full flight — the entire power output advantage of the trap bar jump depends on the bar leaving the ground as the athlete leaves the floor. Loading above the optimal range (typically 10–30% of trap bar 1RM) caps bar velocity and defeats the ballistic mechanism.
common_errors.countermovement_dip_with_spinal_flexion: Initiating the lift with a rapid dip by bending the arms and flexing the spine to create a whip effect — this dangerous technique introduces lumbar flexion under load and can cause disc injury. The starting position should be set with tension in the lats, arms fully extended, and spine neutral before the first pull.
common_errors.not_maintaining_acceleration: Failing to maintain acceleration through the entire lift and into the jump — athletes sometimes treat the trap bar jump as a fast deadlift that happens to get airborne rather than an explosive jump that starts from the floor. Intent should be maximum velocity through terminal hip extension.
common_errors.passive_landing: Landing by crashing down and relaxing the legs rather than controlling eccentric deceleration — the landing is high-impact (bar plus bodyweight) and requires active muscle absorption. Athletes should land the bar gently and decelerate through a controlled quarter-squat.
common_errors.hips_shooting_up_first: Hips rising faster than the bar in the initial pull, converting the movement into a stiff-leg pull — this loses the quad-dominant benefit of the trap bar's neutral center of mass positioning and stresses the lower back. The shoulders and hips should rise together from the set position.

common_errors.shoulder_rowing_to_assist: The single most common kickback error — the shoulder swings forward and back in sync with the dumbbell, effectively turning a triceps isolation exercise into a partial rear-delt row. Only the forearm from elbow to wrist should move; the upper arm must remain fixed and parallel to the floor.
common_errors.dumbbell_version_tension_problem: Dumbbells provide near-zero resistance in the starting position (arm hanging at 90 degrees) because gravity acts parallel to the forearm — the triceps only contracts meaningfully in the last quarter of the ROM. Elite coaches increasingly prefer cable kickbacks for this reason, as cables provide constant tension throughout the full range.
common_errors.rounding_the_lower_back: In the hip-hinge setup, lifters commonly allow the lower back to round as they reach for the weight or fatigue through the set, compressing the lumbar spine under load. A neutral spine with braced core is the clinical standard, and a bench-supported variation is recommended for lifters with lower back issues.
common_errors.insufficient_elbow_height: Failing to raise the upper arm fully parallel to the floor shortens the triceps' working range and prevents complete elbow extension at the top. The elbow must be at least at torso height — and ideally slightly above — to allow the arm to achieve true full extension.
common_errors.weight_too_heavy: Overloading forces the shoulder and body into compensatory movement to assist the too-heavy dumbbell through the range of motion. Because the triceps are only effectively loaded through roughly 50% of the dumbbell kickback ROM, the movement requires relatively light weights to maintain strict isolation.

common_errors.elbow_flare: Allowing the elbows to drift outward from the torso introduces shoulder abduction and shifts load away from the triceps — especially the lateral head. Elbows must track close to the sides throughout the full range of motion to maintain isolation.
common_errors.forward_lean_and_body_English: Leaning heavily forward and using the bodyweight to drive the stack down substitutes gravitational torque for triceps strength and prevents the lateral and medial heads from completing a true full-extension contraction. The torso should be upright or with only a slight forward incline.
common_errors.short_range_of_motion: Not allowing the forearms to return above 90 degrees at the top eliminates the eccentric stretch on the triceps, and not achieving full elbow extension at the bottom omits the peak contraction. Both phases are needed for complete lateral and medial head development.
common_errors.excessive_grip_tension: Death-gripping the attachment causes co-contraction of the forearm flexors and can contribute to lateral epicondyle irritation. A firm but controlled grip allows the forearm muscles to stay relaxed and lets the triceps drive the movement.
common_errors.incorrect_attachment_choice_for_goal: Using the straight bar when targeting the long head (which needs supination to engage fully) is less effective than switching to a rope and flaring at the bottom. Coaches flag this because attachment selection directly determines which triceps head is emphasized.

common_errors.knees_not_reaching_horizontal: Not pulling the knees to or above hip height — the defining demand of the tuck jump is maximal knee flexion at the apex, which requires forceful hip flexor contraction. Athletes who barely lift their knees are performing a simple countermovement jump with no additional hip flexor stimulus.
common_errors.stiff_leg_landing: Touching down with locked or minimally bent knees, which transfers all impact force directly to the joint cartilage and bone rather than through the muscles eccentrically. Knees should absorb the landing through a controlled quarter-squat.
common_errors.excessive_forward_lean: Leaning the torso significantly forward during the tuck — the jump should be predominantly vertical with the center of mass staying roughly over the feet. Forward lean sends the athlete drifting and limits the next rep's jump height.
common_errors.insufficient_jump_height: Failing to achieve adequate flight time before attempting the knee tuck — athletes who rush the tuck without jumping high enough are forced to truncate the hip flexion and cannot complete the movement pattern. The jump must be tall enough to give the hip flexors time to work.
common_errors.asymmetrical_knee_tuck: One knee reaching significantly higher or closer to the chest than the other on each rep — this often reflects a bilateral hip flexor strength imbalance and can indicate or worsen movement pattern asymmetries over time.

common_errors.overstriding: Taking excessively long steps — places enormous stress on the front knee and hip flexors, reduces control and power output, and makes the step-through unstable. Step length should allow the front shin to be approximately vertical at the bottom.
common_errors.knee_valgus: Front knee caving inward during the descent — the same valgus collapse pattern seen in squats, indicating weak hip abductors. Significantly increases ACL and patellofemoral stress. Cue: 'drive the front knee out over the pinky toe.'
common_errors.torso_lean: Excessive forward lean of the torso during the descent — overloads the front knee and reduces the exercise's benefit for the posterior chain. Core should remain upright and braced throughout each step.
common_errors.heel_lift: Front heel coming off the ground during the descent — shifts loading to the forefoot and significantly reduces gluteus maximus and hamstring contribution to the movement. Often indicates poor ankle dorsiflexion mobility.
common_errors.rushing_movement: Moving through reps quickly without controlling each landing and descent — eliminates time under tension, increases the risk of knee and ankle injury on each plant, and reduces the training stimulus to both legs.

common_errors.shoulder_elevation_shrugging: Allowing the shoulder girdle to elevate toward the ears as the arms slide up is the defining error of this exercise — it substitutes upper trapezius and levator scapulae for the intended serratus anterior and lower trapezius activation. The cue is to keep the shoulders down and let the forearms move, not to push with the neck muscles.
common_errors.excessive_lumbar_extension: Arching the lower back away from the wall as the arms reach overhead removes the anterior core stability that is a core biomechanical prerequisite for this exercise's effectiveness. The ribcage and lumbar spine must remain in contact with or neutral relative to the wall throughout.
common_errors.losing_forearm_contact_with_wall: Letting the forearms pull away from the wall reduces the closed-chain serratus anterior demand that makes this exercise superior to open-chain reaching — the constant wall pressure through the forearms is the mechanism that drives scapular upward rotation.
common_errors.insufficient_range_of_motion: Stopping the slide short of full overhead reach reduces serratus anterior activation, which is greatest above 90° of shoulder elevation — this is exactly the position where many impingement patients have pain, making it the therapeutic target of the exercise.
common_errors.wrong_starting_position: Beginning with forearms too far down the wall (below 90° of elbow height) or too wide changes the muscle recruitment pattern and reduces the specificity for lower trapezius and serratus anterior. Starting with forearms roughly at shoulder height and elbows bent 90° is the correct entry position.

common_errors.pushing_off_the_back_foot: Using the trailing foot on the floor to contribute drive to the upward step rather than relying entirely on the front leg that is on the box — this dramatically reduces the unilateral strength stimulus the exercise is designed to develop and allows significant bilateral compensation to mask single-leg weaknesses. The back foot should function only as a balance reference; all force production must come from the working leg. A useful coaching test is to have the athlete hover the back foot slightly off the ground on each rep.
common_errors.using_momentum_and_load_too_heavy: Loading the exercise beyond the athlete's single-leg strength capacity forces them to rock, bounce, or throw the dumbbells to assist upward movement — this eliminates the controlled eccentric and concentric muscle loading and turns the movement into a momentum drill rather than a strength exercise. The appropriate weight produces a challenging but fully controlled repetition in both directions.
common_errors.incomplete_hip_extension_at_top: Failing to fully extend the hip and knee of the working leg at the top of the movement — stopping short of lockout reduces the range of motion trained, limits glute activation at peak contraction, and teaches partial movement patterns. The athlete should reach a fully extended standing position on top of the box, pause briefly, then lower under control.
common_errors.uncontrolled_descent: Dropping the back foot to the floor rapidly rather than lowering slowly through the full range of the working leg sacrifices the eccentric loading phase, which is where significant strength adaptations occur. The descent should be deliberate and controlled, with the working leg's quad and glute resisting gravity throughout, taking 2–3 seconds to reach the floor.
common_errors.inappropriate_box_height: Using a box that is too high for the athlete's current hip mobility and strength — indicated by the pelvis tucking under, the torso collapsing forward excessively, or the knee caving inward during the step — loads the lumbar spine and knee in compromised positions. The correct box height allows the working knee to reach approximately 90 degrees of flexion while maintaining an upright torso and neutral spine throughout the movement.

common_errors.defaulting_to_close_grip_mechanics: Using a wide grip bar but pulling with the same elbow path as a close grip row — the wide grip requires elbows to flare outward to approximately 70–90° to the torso to actually recruit the upper trapezius and rear deltoid. Keeping elbows tucked with a wide grip defeats the purpose of the variation.
common_errors.lumbar_flexion_and_torso_momentum: Rocking the torso forward and backward to generate momentum — identical to standard cable row errors; the torso must stay fixed so the upper back musculature, not the spinal extensors and hip flexors, is generating the movement.
common_errors.pronated_grip_wrist_stress: Using a wide overhand grip without monitoring wrist and elbow comfort — the pronated position places greater stress on the lateral elbow and wrist than a neutral grip; athletes with elbow tendinopathy should be directed to an appropriate attachment angle rather than defaulting to fully pronated.
common_errors.incomplete_scapular_retraction: Pulling the bar to the torso without achieving full rhomboid and mid-trap contraction at end range — the wide grip specifically targets the upper back and interscapular muscles, which require deliberate squeeze and hold at peak contraction to maximally train.
common_errors.ignoring_the_eccentric: Letting the cable pull the arms forward rapidly without controlling the return — the eccentric phase of the wide grip row loads the rhomboids and mid-traps in their lengthening range; rushing through it halves the training stimulus.

common_errors.excessive_range_of_motion_forced: Forcing the wrist into hyperextension at the bottom to increase range beyond what the joint tolerates, particularly under load. This places extreme tensile stress on the common flexor tendon origin at the medial epicondyle and is a primary mechanism for developing medial epicondylitis ('golfer's elbow').
common_errors.forearm_lifting_off_support: Allowing the forearm to rise off the thigh or bench during the curl so the biceps begin assisting. The forearm must remain fully supported and horizontal throughout the rep — if the elbow flexors engage, the wrist flexors are no longer the limiting tissue.
common_errors.grip_tightening_at_bottom: Squeezing the bar maximally in the fully extended position at the bottom rather than allowing the fingers to open and the bar to roll into the fingertips. Full range finger-to-palm rolling substantially increases flexor digitorum recruitment and range of motion; an over-gripped hold shortens the movement and reduces hypertrophic stimulus.
common_errors.excessive_load: Loading the wrist curl as heavily as other arm exercises. The wrist flexors are small muscles with narrow tendons; even trained lifters typically use only 20–40 lb on wrist curls. Overloading causes compensatory elbow flexion and dramatically increases tendinopathy risk.

common_errors.overstriding: Taking large steps to cover ground faster is the most common beginner error — it increases yoke sway, disrupts balance, and slows overall velocity. Elite technique uses short, rapid 'toes-to-heels' steps where the heel of the advancing foot never passes the toes of the planted foot, maximizing stability while maintaining speed.
common_errors.inadequate_core_bracing: Failing to achieve full 360-degree brace before picking up the yoke means the torso lacks the stiffness needed to transfer force from the legs to the implement. McGill's EMG data showed that the yoke imposes the highest spinal compression of any strongman event precisely because massive co-contraction is required to stiffen the torso against the compressive load — any lapse in bracing dramatically increases injury risk.
common_errors.yoke_sway: Allowing the yoke crossbar to swing laterally during movement, which amplifies effective load and disrupts stride pattern. Athletes should grip the uprights (not just the crossbar) to gain lateral control, and use short steps to minimize the pendulum effect of the heavily loaded implement.
common_errors.setup_bar_height_neglect: Not adjusting the crossbar height to the athlete — too low forces excessive forward lean and quad-dominant pickup; too high requires dangerous tiptoe positioning. The bar should sit in the same position as a high-bar back squat to allow a safe, powerful pick-up with full hip extension.
common_errors.slowing_before_finish: Decelerating before the designated finish distance — a critical competition error since the athlete who drops the yoke last wins. Athletes must maintain stride frequency to the line and only decelerate once the implement is past the mark.

common_errors.ballistic_wrist_rotation: Snapping the wrists rapidly from supinated to pronated at the top of the curl rather than rotating in a slow, controlled manner. Uncontrolled rotational loading at the top of the movement places high torque on the distal radio-ulnar joint and the wrist capsule; the rotation should take 1–2 seconds and remain within pain-free range.
common_errors.elbow_drift: Allowing the elbows to drift forward during the supinated concentric phase, which recruits the anterior deltoid to assist and reduces biceps long-head stretch stimulus. The elbows must stay fixed at the sides throughout the entire repetition — the Zottman is an elbow flexion exercise, not a partial shoulder press.
common_errors.using_full_reverse_curl_weight: Loading the dumbbells as heavily as a standard reverse curl because you figure the pronated phase is the goal. The eccentric pronated phase must handle the same weight that was curled supinated (which is heavier than a reverse curl could manage concentrically), so weight should be selected based on the ability to control the descent pronated — not on concentric supinated strength.
common_errors.incomplete_supination: Starting the concentric phase with a neutral or semi-pronated grip rather than fully supinating the forearm. Full supination maximizes biceps brachii recruitment by engaging its supination function alongside elbow flexion; a neutral starting position converts the concentric phase into a hammer curl and defeats the purpose of the exercise.
